articles.title: Pesquisa Quaest: 44% temem volta de Bolsonaro e 42% reeleição de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa mostra que medo de uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro voltou a ser maior numericamente, o que não acontecia desde agosto na série da Quaest.
articles.summary: Pesquisa Quaest revela que o medo da volta da família Bolsonaro ao poder superou numericamente o receio de uma reeleição de Lula.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21) mostra que 44% dos eleitores têm medo da volta da família Bolsonaro com a possível vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), ao mesmo tempo em que outros 42% têm medo da reeleição de Lula (PT). O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.

Em relação à última edição da pesquisa, da semana passada , houve um empate entre os que temiam a volta dos Bolsonaro ao poder e uma reeleição de Lula.

Houve um aumento entre os que possuem medo dos dois: no levantamento anterior, eram 3%. Agora, são 6%. O número dos que dizem não ter medo de nenhum oscilou para baixo, de 6% para 4%.

O medo do retorno da família Bolsonaro não ultrapassava numericamente a reeleição do petista desde o levantamento de 14 de agosto. Naquela , 45% temiam o retorno da família Bolsonaro com uma eventual vitória de Flávio. Já 41% temiam a continuidade do PT no governo.

A Quaest mostra também que a maior diferença entre os que temem Flávio Bolsonaro e os que temem Lula se dá na parcela dos beneficiários do Bolsa Família. Neste caso, 63% temem o retorno da família Bolsonaro. Antes, eram 58%. Já 23% temem um novo mandato de Lula. No levantamento anterior, eram 29%.

Não soube ou não quis responder: 4% (era 5%)

O que dá mais medo hoje? | Beneficiários do Bolsa Família

A volta da família Bolsonaro ao poder: 63% (era 58%)

Segundo o levantamento, o cenário de intenção de voto para o segundo turno da disputa presidencial é o seguinte:

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL): 45% (eram 46% há uma semana)

Os dois candidatos estão em empate técnico dentro da margem de erro, que é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos.

📋Segundo os dados registrados no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), foram entrevistadas 2.154 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 17 e 20 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada como BR-08535/2026.

Candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula participam de debate da Band antes do 2º turno das eleições. — Foto: REUTERS/Jean Carniel

articles.title: Pesquisa Quaest 2º turno: Flávio Bolsonaro tem 45% e Lula 44% | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidatos estão em empate técnico, com diferença de 1 ponto percentual. Pesquisa divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21) foi encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.
articles.summary: Pesquisa Quaest 2º turno mostra Flávio Bolsonaro com 45% e Lula com 44% das intenções de voto, configurando empate técnico na disputa presidencial.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest do segundo turno, divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21), mostra Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) com 45% das intenções de voto, contra 44% de Lula . A situação é de empate técnico, com 1 ponto de diferença entre os dois candidatos.

A pesquisa foi encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo. Veja os números:

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL): 45% (eram 46% há uma semana)

Quaest: 2º turno: estimulada — Foto: Arte/g1

Em relação à pesquisa Quaest anterior, divulgada há uma semana, no dia 14, Flávio Bolsonaro oscilou um ponto para baixo (tinha 46%) e Lula manteve os 44%. A situação já era de empate técnico e assim se manteve. O percentual de votos em branco, nulos e de pessoas que não vão votar se manteve em 9%. Os indecisos passaram de 1% para 2%.

🔎 Em pesquisas eleitorais, o empate técnico acontece quando candidatos têm uma diferença de pontuação menor do que a margem de erro. Na Quaest, a margem é de dois pontos para mais ou para menos. Ou seja, se a diferença entre os candidatos for de até quatro pontos, a situação é de empate técnico.

Veja como está a diferença de intenção de voto entre Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula considerando a margem de erro:

Gráfico mostra intervalos de intenções de voto de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro, considerando a margem de erro — Foto: Reprodução/Quaest

📋 A pesquisa Quaest de 20 de outubro ouviu 2.154 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 17 e 20 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) como BR-08535/2026.

De uma semana para outra, a rejeição a Lula caiu de 53% para 47% . A rejeição a Flávio Bolsonaro oscilou dois pontos para baixo, de 54% para 52%.

Quaest, 2º turno: rejeição dos candidatos à Presidência — Foto: Arte/g1

A Quaest mostra também a transferência de votos do primeiro para o segundo turno, com as evoluções desde a pesquisa anterior, de uma semana atrás.

A margem de erro para esses recortes varia e é maior, porque são grupos menores de eleitores.

Gráfico mostra transferência de votos e variação em relação à pesquisa anterior — Foto: Reprodução/Quaest

Eleitores de Ronaldo Caiado (margem de erro: 24 pontos)

Flávio Bolsonaro: passou de 40% para 51%

Branco/nulo/não vai votar: passou de 43% para 24%

Eleitores que não votaram ou votaram em branco/nulo (margem de erro: 6 pontos)

Flávio Bolsonaro: passou de 38% para 36%

Branco/nulo/não vai votar: passou de 17% para 21%

Na pesquisa espontânea, quando os eleitores entrevistados respondem sem ver os nomes dos candidatos, Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula têm 40% cada um.

O número de indecisos passou de 7% para 14% desde a semana passada, e o percentual de votos em branco e nulos variou de 8% para 6%.

Entre as mulheres, o percentual de indecisos passou de 8% para 17%. Entre os eleitores independentes -- que não são nem petistas nem bolsonaristas, nem de direita nem de esquerda --, a parcela de indecisos foi de 13% para 31%.

A Quest perguntou aos eleitores se a decisão de voto deles era definitiva ou se ainda podia mudar. Veja o que os entrevistados responderam:

Entre eleitores de Lula, 90% dizem que a decisão é definitiva e 9%, que ainda podem mudar o voto. Entre eleitores de Flávio Bolsonaro, os números são 93% e 7%, respectivamente.

Entre os entrevistados, 54% acham que Flávio Bolsonaro vai vencer a disputa (eram 53% na pesquisa anterior), e 37% apontam Lula como favorito (eram 35%).

articles.title: PT e PL assinam carta conjunta por respeito durante carreata | G1
articles.standfirst: Documento foi assinado na segunda-feira (19) pelos presidentes dos dois partidos em Itapetininga (SP). Apelo feito em conjunto aos apoiadores pede respeito, civilidade e responsabilidade.
articles.summary: O Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) e o Partido Liberal (PL) assinaram uma carta conjunta pedindo por respeito durante a realização de uma carreata em Itapetininga (SP).
articles.body:
Eleitores de Itapetininga (SP) voltam às urnas neste domingo (25 para o 2º turno — Foto: Carla Monteiro/TV TEM

O Partido dos Trabalhadores ( PT ) e o Partido Liberal ( PL ) em Itapetininga (SP) assinaram uma carta conjunta pedindo por respeito e pela democracia nesses últimos dias de campanha antes do segundo turno das eleições para presidente, que ocorrem neste domingo (25) em todo o país.

A carta aberta foi assinada pelos presidentes dos partidos na cidade, Rafael Simões (PT) e Milton Júnior (PL), na segunda-feira (19) e publicada nas redes sociais na noite desta quinta-feira (20).

Os dois partidos estão na disputa do segundo turno, representados pelos candidatos Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro , respectivamente. A mensagem principal do texto é a defesa da democracia, do respeito e convivência pacífica entre os leitores. ( Confira abaixo a íntegra da carta .)

Os partidos afirmaram que defender uma candidatura, expressar opiniões e participar da vida política são direitos de todos. Mas reforçam que, nenhuma divergência justifica a intolerância, hostilidade ou qualquer forma de violência.

PT e PL assinam carta conjunta por respeito durante carreata realizada em Itapetininga — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

À população, eles pediram que uma carreata que será realizada em Itapetininga seja um momento para que os cidadãos tenham o direito de demonstrar suas convicções políticas. Os presidentes municipais dos partidos fizeram um apelo aos apoiadores, que no ato do evento, seja prevalecido o respeito, a civilidade e a responsabilidade.

No documento, eles apontaram que adversários políticos não podem ser considerados inimigos e que atitudes como ofensas e confrontos também não contribuem para o debate político. Além de não representar os valores democráticos.

Ao fim da carta, os representantes reforçaram o pedido de que a carreata seja marcada pela participação popular e o exercício pacífico da democracia.

PT e PL assinam carta pedindo respeito durante última semana de campanha eleitoral para o 2º turno das Eleições em Itapetininga (SP) — Foto: Desirèe Assis/g1

Confira abaixo o conteúdo da carta na íntegra:

"Em defesa da democracia, do respeito e da convivência pacífica.

A democracia se fortalece quando somos capazes de conviver com nossas diferenças. Defender uma candidatura, expressar opiniões e participar da vida política são direitos de todos. Nenhuma divergência, por mais profunda que seja, justifica a intolerância, a hostilidade ou qualquer forma de violência.

Neste sábado, 24 de outubro, as campanhas presidenciais realizarão carreatas em Itapetininga. Será um momento de manifestação democrática, em que cada cidadão terá o direito de demonstrar livremente suas convicções políticas.

Nós, presidentes municipais do Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) e do Partido Liberal (PL), representando campos políticos distintos, fazemos um apelo conjunto aos nossos apoiadores: que prevaleçam o respeito, a civilidade e a responsabilidade.

Adversários políticos não são inimigos. A liberdade de manifestação de um grupo deve ser respeitada pelo outro. Provocações, ofensas, ameaças e confrontos não contribuem para o debate público e não representam os valores democráticos que devem orientar nossa sociedade.

A disputa eleitoral é passageira. A convivência entre familiares, amigos, vizinhos e cidadãos permanece. Independentemente do resultado das urnas, continuaremos compartilhando a mesma cidade, os mesmos espaços públicos e a responsabilidade de construir uma Itapetininga melhor.

Que o próximo sábado seja marcado pela alegria, pela participação popular e pelo exercício pacífico da democracia.

Podemos discordar nas escolhas políticas e permanecer unidos no respeito à democracia."

articles.title: Pesquisa Quaest: 47% desaprovam governo Lula e 46% aprovam | G1
articles.standfirst: Margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos. Pesquisa divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21) foi encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.
articles.summary: Pesquisa Quaest avaliou a aprovação e desaprovação do governo Lula. A pesquisa mostra também que há um empate técnico na disputa pela Presidência.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21) mostra que 47% desaprovam e 46% aprovam o governo do presidente Lula , candidato à reeleição pelo PT.

Em relação à pesquisa anterior , a desaprovação oscilou um ponto para baixo, de 48% para 47%, e a aprovação variou um ponto para cima, de 45% para 46%.

A diferença entre os dois índices eram de três pontos e diminuiu para um ponto. Com isso, fica dentro da margem de erro de dois pontos percentuais.

A avaliação negativa oscilou para baixo, de 40% para 38%. A avaliação positiva se manteve em 34%. Outros 26% consideram o governo regular (eram 24% na pesquisa anterior).

O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo. A Quaest entrevistou 2.154 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 17 e 20 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é BR-08535/2026.

A Quaest mostra também que Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) tem 45% das intenções de voto, contra 44% de Lula . Permanece o empate técnico entre os candidatos a poucos dias do segundo turno.

Desaprova: 47% (eram 48% na pesquisa anterior)

Negativa: 38% (eram 40% na pesquisa anterior)

Quaest: avaliação do governo Lula — Foto: Arte/g1

articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) — Foto: Reprodução/Divulgação das campanhas

Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (21) mostra que 47% dos eleitores afirmam que não votariam em Lula (PT) de jeito nenhum. O percentual era de 53% na rodada anterior, divulgada em 14 de outubro.

Já a rejeição à Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) é de 52%, ante 54% na pesquisa anterior.

Entre as mulheres , 57% afirmam que não votariam em Flávio Bolsonaro, enquanto 42% rejeitam Lula. Já entre os homens, a rejeição ao petista é de 53%, e a de Flávio Bolsonaro, de 46%.

No recorte por religião , 60% dos evangélicos dizem que não votariam em Lula de jeito nenhum, enquanto 37% rejeitam Flávio Bolsonaro. Entre os católicos, 58% rejeitam o candidato do PL, e 41%, o presidente.

articles.title: TSE e Meta: disputa sobre algoritmos marca reta final da eleição | G1
articles.standfirst: A poucos dias do segundo turno, TSE amplia discussões com a Meta enquanto campanhas de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro travam batalha judicial sobre supostos impactos de algoritmos e moderação.
articles.summary: Na reta final do segundo turno, o TSE amplia o diálogo com a Meta enquanto as campanhas de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro questionam o impacto dos algoritmos.
articles.body:
A quatro dias das eleições, o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) intensificou as discussões com representantes da Meta e das campanhas eleitorais para esclarecer questionamentos sobre o funcionamento dos algoritmos das redes sociais e possíveis prejuízos aos candidatos. O cenário é marcado por uma série de disputas judiciais envolvendo o uso das plataformas digitais na campanha.

Em reunião realizada na noite desta terça-feira, representantes da Meta, advogados das campanhas de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) e Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) e integrantes da Justiça Eleitoral discutiram os questionamentos apresentados pelos partidos. O encontro ocorreu após uma ação do PT que alegou prejuízos à campanha do presidente Lula relacionados à atuação da plataforma.

A reunião foi conduzida para esclarecer as posições da empresa e permitir que os envolvidos apresentassem dúvidas antes de uma eventual conclusão sobre o caso.

A campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro também procurou se posicionar na discussão. A equipe do candidato afirma que enfrenta prejuízos relacionados à atuação da Meta e busca evitar que apenas o PT seja considerado prejudicado.

A disputa pode ganhar novos desdobramentos jurídicos, inclusive com medidas de maior alcance que, dependendo do caso, podem resultar em sanções eleitorais.

Além da discussão envolvendo a Meta, as campanhas protagonizam uma série de iniciativas judiciais relacionadas à circulação de conteúdo político nas redes sociais e à atuação dos algoritmos.

Na noite desta terça-feira, houve uma nova petição direcionada ao presidente do TSE, Kassio Nunes Marques, sobre questões envolvendo canais associados ao entorno da campanha de Lula, incluindo referências ao deputado André Janones.

O caso já havia passado por diferentes decisões judiciais, com intervenções do ministro e da Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça Eleitoral.

A sucessão de decisões e recursos mostra a complexidade das disputas sobre a propaganda eleitoral na internet. Também houve uma nova iniciativa da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro alegando uma suposta manipulação de algoritmos do Google.

O cenário levanta questionamentos sobre a capacidade da Justiça Eleitoral de responder, em tempo hábil, aos desafios impostos pelas plataformas digitais .

Embora a inteligência artificial tenha sido apontada como uma das principais preocupações do processo eleitoral, as discussões sobre os algoritmos e seus possíveis efeitos sobre o alcance das campanhas ganharam destaque na reta final.

Ainda não há uma conclusão definitiva sobre quais candidaturas teriam sido prejudicadas nem sobre a dimensão de eventuais impactos no resultado eleitoral. Mesmo assim, a discussão pode continuar depois da votação e ser utilizada pelas campanhas em novas iniciativas judiciais, inclusive por candidatos derrotados.

A relevância da Meta no processo eleitoral também está relacionada ao volume de recursos destinados à publicidade digital. A empresa controla Instagram , Facebook e WhatsApp , plataformas que ocupam posições importantes na comunicação política, embora os formatos de anúncios e as possibilidades de impulsionamento variem entre elas.

Os gastos das campanhas com a Meta cresceram significativamente nos últimos anos . Em 2018, o montante gasto com a empresa era de aproximadamente R$ 23 milhões. Na prestação de contas parcial do ciclo eleitoral de 2026, o valor já chega a cerca de R$ 290 milhões.

A pressão sobre a empresa também envolve seu Comitê de Supervisão , órgão independente criado a partir de uma iniciativa anunciada em 2018 e implementada em 2020. O colegiado reúne especialistas de diferentes áreas e conta com a participação do brasileiro Ronaldo Lemos.

Na declaração divulgada nesta terça-feira (20), o conselho afirmou que “está preocupado com as falhas recorrentes na aplicação das normas eleitorais da Meta” e afirmou que a empresa precisa fazer mais para garantir que suas práticas de fiscalização durante as eleições sejam transparentes e consistentes.

articles.title: Criticism grows over Ramaswamy attack ad featuring Amy Acton's mother
articles.summary: Several Ohio politicians have taken to social media to condemn an attack ad against Amy Acton that featured her estranged mother.
articles.body:
A chorus of condemnation from some Ohio politicians is growing against Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over an attack ad produced by his campaign that featured his opponent's estranged mother criticizing her and questioning the years of abuse she endured as a child.

The ad, which has not been aired on television but spread on social media, shows Dr. Amy Acton's estranged mother, Donna Stearns Arthur, criticizing Acton, calling her a liar and casting doubt on Acton's upbringing. Acton has been estranged from Arthur since 1978 when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, faced a rape charge for sexually assaulting Acton when she was 12 years old.

Cledith died in southern Pennsylvania and was never convicted of the charge, and Acton's mother stayed married to him until his death.

Vivek Ramaswamy's career in photos, from business to politics

A clip of the ad, which blogger The Rooster shared on social media on Oct. 19 , shows Arthur accusing her daughter of lying about Acton's upbringing, which included homelessness, neglect and abuse, and urging Ohioans not to vote for Acton. "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem," Arthur says in the ad. "She is a liar. She lies about her past."

Acton's brother, Phillip Stearns, condemned the ad, and said Ramaswamy "stooped to a despicable low" in attempting to turn Acton's abuse into a "political talking point."

"After [Cledith] was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said of Arthur. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

The Acton campaign released an ad later Oct. 20 of Acton's brother berating Ramaswamy over the ad, and saying that "Amy took the brunt of [the abuse]."

Acton told WOSU that her mother is the one lying. "It's awful to see her this way, and it's even more incredible to see that my opponent [Ramaswamy] has taken advantage of someone who's clearly not well, who is older, and this is totally in line with who he is," Acton told WOSU.

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, doubled down on support for the ad and accused Acton of being a "serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."

"Her mother has spoken out for years and I don't know Amy Acton's mother and I've never met Amy Acton either," Ramaswamy said. "What I do know is that Amy Acton has been repeatedly and serially dishonest during this campaign and for much of her record in public service and I do believe that that record deserves to be scrutinized."

Several prominent Democrats – including State Rep. Allison Russo, D-Upper Arlington, who is running for Ohio Secretary of State, and Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell, who is running for state auditor against Secretary of State Frank LaRose – called on Ohio Republicans in an Oct. 20 media release to condemn the ad, calling it a "new and unacceptable low in Ohio politics."

"Every single Republican candidate running for statewide office should immediately and publicly denounce this ad," Russo and other Democrats said in the media release "Silence in the face of such destructive rhetoric is an endorsement of it. It is time to raise the standard of public discourse in Ohio and focus on the practical solutions our citizens deserve."

David Axelrod, a political consultant and CNN analyst, also took to X to condemn Ramaswamy and said that he had an "unquenchable ambition" to become Ohio's next governor.

"I've been around politics longer than [Ramaswamy's] been alive, and I don't think I've seen anything uglier," Axelrod wrote.

The growing condemnation from both Democrats and some Republicans is part of the larger conversations swirling around campaign ads in Ohio. Campaigns have spent more than $450 million on ads, according to AdImpact, and have become more inflammatory and exaggerated as the respective races drag on.

Jerry Miller, a professor of communication studies at Ohio University and an expert in political communications, told The Dispatch that while campaign advertising may appear especially combative this election season, its underlying purpose remains largely unchanged: to draw sharp contrasts, undermine opponents and shape voters' perceptions.

Miller said that dynamic is particularly evident in the contest between Ramaswamy and Acton, neither of whom has previously held elected office. As a result, he said, campaign attacks are more likely to focus on questions of credibility, character and public image rather than records in elected office.

Although the ad never formally aired on television, Miller said it still served multiple strategic purposes. On one hand, it sought to discredit Amy Acton; on the other, it initially provided Ramaswamy with a measure of plausible deniability because it was circulated on social media.

Miller said the ad's online circulation may have been intentional, arguing that the attention generated by its release, including coverage from national media outlets such as the New York Times and ABC News has helped amplify its message and spark public discussion even without a traditional television rollout.

"What is especially troubling with this ad is the subject matter and its use of a woman, presumably Amy Acton's mother, to deliver the allegations," Miller said in an email to The Dispatch.

"Whether or not the ad was ever meant to air in major media markets, the attention it draws, from news outlets that cover it to scholars like me who study political advertising and communication, lends it a measure of legitimacy and widens its audience," he said. "That makes it a strategically effective move for whoever is behind it."

Director of Ohio Department of Development says 'there are lines we shouldn't cross'

Lydia Mihalik, director of the Ohio Department of Development, said the ad crossed lines that shouldn't have been crossed.

"We can disagree on plenty of things without losing our sense of decency," Mihalik wrote on her X account.

Meghan McCain, daughter of the late John McCain, condemns ad

"This is a dastardly ad," Meghan McCain, the daughter of the late 2008 presidential nominee John McCain, said on X.

"It should never have been created. Shame on whatever consultant firm created this."

U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown calls on opponent to condemn ad

"The ad released by Vivek Ramaswamy is disgusting," Brown said. "Everyone, including Jon Husted, should be willing to condemn this ad."

Libertarian candidate for Ohio governor speaks out

"You don't weaponize someone's personal history of being a victim of abuse against them – and then shift gears and gaslight everyone about the situation – unless you, yourself, have an abusive personality. That is Vivek Ramaswamy and the Ohio Republican Party," said Don Kissick, the Libertarian candidate for Ohio governor.

Chuck Todd, former host of Meet the Press

"Imagine knowing these circumstances and deciding to green light this ad anyway. We are so numb to the gutter politics of this era that it's sometimes hard to shock but I have a feeling Mike DeWine and John Kasich Republicans are going to be disgusted with Ramaswamy on this one and it costs him more votes than Acton."

"Amy Acton's stepfather never stood trial and never faced a conviction after Amy Acton accused him of rape. He was accused. He was never convicted," she said.

"We have seen over and over again how anyone can accuse someone of rape. They did it to Brett Kavanaugh. They did it to President Trump. Liberal women love accusing men of rape."

"When the message is true and the Left doesn't like it, what do they do? Discredit the messenger of course!"

articles.title: Secret Service study explores how to prevent workplace violence
articles.summary: The law enforcement agency best known for protecting the president is using its knowledge to prevent attacks.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Secret Service, best known for protecting presidents and dignitaries, is leveraging its vast intelligence gathering, research capabilities and other tools to help prevent workplace violence. A new report seen by NBC News from the Secret Service’s National Threat Assessment Center analyzed 50 cases of workplace violence over the past decade to seek common motivations, tactics and warning signs, including the shooting at the Capital Gazette in 2018 in Annapolis, Maryland, in which a gunman killed five employees. In the incidents under review, 119 were killed and 128 were injured. The report was born of the center’s examination of mass attacks, which found most of the targeted locations were businesses. “Which is why we launched this initiative,” said Lina Alathari, who leads the threat assessment center. “To look at how can we prevent targeted workplace violence. What is the thinking, behavior and circumstances of workplace attackers?” The threat assessment center was developed to study how other kinds of attacks could be prevented. Officials use that knowledge and apply it in other situations, such as school shootings, mass attacks and now workplace violence. The report, expected to be released Wednesday, is intended to provide guidance to businesses, human resources officials, local law enforcement agencies and mental health professionals who mitigate workplace risks. Alathari said there are almost always warning signs before someone attacks. While the reviewed cases do not suggest that attackers belong to any specific demographic group, they do share similar patterns. “Grievances are always the No. 1 motive that might sort of trigger someone to carry out an attack,” Alathari said. Retail and service businesses are the most frequently attacked, because the public often has easy access, followed by manufacturing and healthcare facilities. The connection between a targeted business and a perpetrator is typically direct and personal; 16 of the attackers were actively employed at the sites they targeted. Others are tied through current or estranged romantic partners, she said. According to the Secret Service’s research, more than 40% of the suspects in cases of such violence had histories of domestic violence, but they were not always charged with crimes related to that violence, the report found. Given the prevalence of violence against intimate partners, the study urges workplaces to recognize signs and support employees. “That includes empowering those who may be experiencing stalking, harassing, threats from romantic partners or other relatives to feel connected enough to come forward and ask for help,” Alathari said. Most of the attackers used firearms, but others used knives, explosives or vehicles. Nearly 25% of the attacks involved more than one weapon. The resolutions of the incidents varied; in more than 75% of them, attackers stopped causing harm on their own and were arrested at the scene. Nearly half died by suicide. In 14% of the studied cases, law enforcement ended the violence by killing the suspect. The National Threat Assessment Center Team described one case in which the suspect had been fired but the employee’s badge access remained active and allowed the attacker to return and gain access. It advised people to look for common warning signs: changes in behavior, depression, increased absenteeism, discussion of weapons, expression of violent thoughts or any kind of threats against co-workers. Last year, the Secret Service led 400 training sessions on preventing mass violence for roughly 50,000 participants nationwide. “There are always opportunities for intervention, and what I can tell you is that the cost of inaction can be deadly,” Alathari said.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: The 5 factors that could decide Michigan's tight and ugly senate race
articles.summary: Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed face five decisive factors in the final two weeks of Michigan's razor-thin 2026 midterm senate race showdown.
articles.body: The Michigan Senate race between Republican candidate Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has turned into the marquee matchup of the 2026 midterms, both as a test of the far left’s ability to compete in middle America and as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s leadership. So what will tip the balance? While many of the basic factors of this contest have already been built in, such as El-Sayed’s disdain for Israel, and Rogers' somewhat qualified support for the president’s policies, there are a few points emerging that could prove decisive in the final two weeks. MORNING GLORY: THE POLLS GOT MICHIGAN BADLY WRONG. NOW DEMOCRATS MAY FACE A BIGGER RECKONING Here are five factors that still could sway who some late deciders vote for, or whether they turn out to vote at all. 1. Temperament Policy differences aside, Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed are very different people with very different temperaments, and voters Fox News Digital spoke with in Michigan could see, in the same temperamental attributes, either a positive or negative light. For example, Leon in Detroit, a city employee in his 40s who supported El-Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens in the primary, said of El-Sayed, "He just comes off arrogant, like he’s talking down to everybody," but young voters I spoke with in Grand Rapids called this attitude, "confidence" and "assertiveness." DAVID MARCUS: WHY ABDUL EL-SAYED’S ANTI-BILLIONAIRE SCREEDS MAY NOT PLAY IN GRAND RAPIDS On the ground, one could almost describe the race as a Thanksgiving dinner in which Rogers is your calm, conservative, wealthy uncle and El-Sayed is the new college boyfriend who keeps talking about how terrible American capitalism is and why the football game on TV is toxic. Michigan voters must choose who they hope will be there next year. LEE CARTER: 2026 ELECTION COULD ALL COME DOWN TO JUST ONE TYPE OF VOTER 2. Get Out The Vote Campaigns Back in August, when El-Sayed won a one-point victory over Stevens, despite polls showing him up by double digits, it was the aggressive far left ground game, especially in semi-urban areas like Dearborn, from groups like the Democratic Socialists of America that saved his bacon. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS As Tiffany Justice, senior advisor for Citizen’s Alliance, told Fox News Digital, "Michigan elections are won at the margins, and the voters who decide them are working-class conservatives who agree with us but don't have a habit of voting. A TV ad won't get them there. A neighbor knocking on their door, looking them in the eye, and personally inviting them to the polls will." Rogers claims that the GOP ground game has been improving in the Wolverine State, and he better hope so. In fact, the money men on the right might need to shift a bit from ads on screens to faces at screen doors. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG 3. Donald Trump You didn’t really think we could leave the president out of this, did you? El-Sayed has dared Trump to campaign with Rogers in Michigan, and Trump has decided to oblige him with a rally set for Sunday, October 25, just a day after former President Barack Obama will rally with El-Sayed. MIKE ROGERS PRESSES CNN'S DANA BASH ON WHY THE PRESS IS 'EAGER' TO DEFEND ABDUL EL-SAYED Rogers, for his part, has distanced himself from Trump both on the conflict in Iran and on the Canadian tariff war, and notably has done so with no blowback from the commander in chief. A Trump rally will bring out much-needed MAGA voters, but it could also alienate independent voters just days before the election. 4. French Riots El-Sayed’s family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, as well as his past statements in support of it, have become central to this race, even after El-Sayed’s hand-waving "sort of" disavowal of the group in a testy town hall exchange, and the backdrop to this issue is the pro-Islamist riots in France. COULD FRANCE'S RIOTS HAPPEN HERE? EXPERTS SEE PARALLELS IN SOCIALISM, IMMIGRATION — AND KEY DIFFERENCES Americans, including voters in Michigan, are increasingly looking towards Europe, with its burning buildings in Limoges and trampling of free speech in London, as a warning of what happens when a nation has untrammeled immigration without assimilation. LIZ PEEK: TWO TROUBLED SENATE RACES COULD SPOIL DEMOCRATS' BLUE-WAVE FANTASY If these riots persist and get worse, both Rogers and El-Sayed will have to address them and the undertones will be clear as day to Michigan voters. 5. The Final Debate On Wednesday, Rogers and El-Sayed will take the stage for their second and final debate, the first having been contentious, but arguably without a knockout blow for either man. The electorate is much more keyed in than it was on October 8, when they first sparred, making this the biggest chance either side has to attract new votes. In a race this close, one viral moment could make all the difference. articles.title: Inside Democrats’ oversight playbook for Trump’s final 2 years
articles.summary: After two years operating from the sidelines, Democrats on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee are planning to conduct ambitious investigations into President Trump and his administration if the lower chamber changes hands in next month’s elections. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who’s in line to chair the powerful committee if Democrats win the gavels,…
articles.body:
After two years operating from the sidelines, Democrats on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee are planning to conduct ambitious investigations into President Trump and his administration if the lower chamber changes hands in next month’s elections.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who’s in line to chair the powerful committee if Democrats win the gavels, is readying a host of probes across a range of topics, including Trump’s ties to the Jeffrey Epstein scandal; changes in vaccine policy under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.; and the killing of U.S. citizens by federal immigration officers.

Garcia is also promising intense scrutiny of Trump’s personal and family finances, which have grown enormously over the past two years with help from Trump’s official actions from the White House.

“There’s so much to look at,” Garcia told reporters in Washington, just before the preelection recess.

The Oversight probes are by no means the only investigations Democrats are planning next year. Nearly every other committee is also eyeing designs to scrutinize some aspect of Trump’s actions, which have been left virtually unchecked while Republicans have controlled Congress.

But the Oversight Committee will play a leading role in that process. And in the majority, Democrats would have extensive new authorities, including the power of subpoena to seek documents and call witnesses, setting the stage for explosive hearings through the final two years of Trump’s presidency.

Here are the five areas where Oversight Democrats say they’ll focus their attention.

On the campaign trail, Trump had supported the release of all the federal files related to Epstein, the convicted sex offender. But after taking office, the president reversed course amid mounting evidence that his personal ties to Epstein were much closer than previously known.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has released millions of files over the last year, in response to a law mandating that disclosure, and DOJ says it has nothing more to share. But Democrats and Epstein victims say the administration is still shielding the names of other Epstein associates who might have committed crimes with minors but were never charged.

“We are absolutely going to be aggressive,” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), an Oversight member, told NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo this month. “We are going to enforce our subpoenas. We are going to issue subpoenas to people who have evaded our questions.”

Some of the individuals who have testified before the committee include former President Bill Clinton, former Epstein assistant Sarah Kellen and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. Subramanyam noted that most of the interviews were voluntary and not done under oath.

“Some of the witnesses decided not to answer certain questions or hand over certain documents, so we’re only scraping the surface of the investigation that we could be doing,” he said.

Under Chair James Comer (R-Ky.), the Oversight Committee has also sought information from Leon Black, a billionaire investor. In September, the House voted unanimously to hold Black in contempt of Congress for defying a subpoena, and Garcia said he’ll keep pressing next year.

“He did not produce what’s been asked for by the subpoena,” Garcia said.

Trump’s personal wealth has soared to $6.6 billion over the last two years, up from $2.4 billion in 2024, according to Forbes .

Much of the gains come from Trump’s meme coin and his family’s broader interests in cryptocurrency, an industry that’s thrived as Trump has relaxed regulations and gutted enforcement by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Trump’s GOP allies say it’s just another example of Trump’s business savvy. But Democrats say it’s open corruption, accusing the president of using his powers to enrich himself.

Their investigations will explore not only Trump’s personal interests, but those of his close associates, his sons and other family members. That includes Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, who is serving as a lead negotiator in the effort to end the Russia-Ukraine War. The effort is reportedly poised to benefit a wealthy Trump donor and Middle Eastern businessmen with ties to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, a longtime Trump associate.

“It’s going to be Jared Kushner, it’s going to be the Trump sons,” Garcia said.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a senior member of the Oversight Committee, is also the top Democrat on the special House committee overseeing China policy. He said he’s ready to dive into the details of another deal that led the United Arab Emirates to invest billions of dollars in the crypto enterprise run by the Trump and Witkoff families, which came just as the White House approved the sale of valuable computer chips to the UAE.

“On the China Committee, as ranking member, I will be looking at the Trump family’s crypto corruption that could have led to the export of chips to UAE and we will aggressively ensure that Chinese companies don’t take our auto market and that we protect American farmers, workers, manufacturers, and unions,” Khanna said in a statement. “I will also look at whether there has been pay to play, including allegations of getting waivers or favorable policies regarding China from companies who supported the Trump ballroom or the administration.”

For two years, Democrats have bashed Trump’s health policies under Kennedy, the nation’s most prominent vaccine skeptic and secretary of the Health and Human Services Department (HHS).

Next year, given the chance, they’re vowing to dig deeper into Kennedy’s most controversial decisions, including the purge of a leading immunization advisory board and revisions to vaccine schedules that defy the official recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics. Democrats suspect that conservative, anti-vax interest groups are driving those decisions, and they’re likely to subpoena any communications between those groups and the administration.

“RFK Jr. is working to destroy our health system in this country,” Garcia said.

From atop the HHS, Kennedy has promoted the idea that vaccines cause autism, a conspiracy theory that has no basis in medical science. He’s championed a vast reduction in funding for the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other subagencies overseeing public health research and outreach. And he also dismissed all 17 members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, replacing them with a new slate of handpicked panelists, many of whom share his views on vaccines.

The Democratic scrutiny may extend to international health concerns as well. In January, responding to a Trump executive order, the United States withdrew from the World Health Organization after 78 years. In doing so, the administration said the group had mishandled the COVID-19 pandemic in ways that benefited China.

Democrats have been clamoring for an overhaul of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol following the deaths of multiple U.S. citizens and immigrants at the hands of federal immigration officers across the country.

Just this year, the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse and U.S. citizen, by a Border Patrol agent and the death of Renee Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen, by an ICE official led Democrats to oppose any new Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding until immigration reforms were made, causing the longest partial government shutdown in U.S. history.

Republicans ultimately passed ICE and Border Patrol funding through the reconciliation process, which bypasses the Senate filibuster. But Democrats want accountability for those deaths, and they’re likely to demand testimony from those directly involved.

During a press conference Monday, Garcia highlighted the poor conditions of immigrants at ICE detention centers, including reports of people being denied their medications and served inedible food, as well as the deportation of people to countries they’ve never been to.

“We have documented over 1000 instances of credible, verifiable abuse by federal immigration agents, and though that documentation is going to lead our work moving forward, I want to make it very clear that in these upcoming elections, the stakes are high, and one issue is whether we’re going to have checks and balances in our government,” Garcia said.

Garcia added that the Oversight Committee will look into the serious allegations of “pay-to-play by people like Corey Lewandowski and Kristi Noem, where we know that human beings are being used to line the pockets of the wealthiest corporations, private companies, where they make a profit off every person that is being picked up off of our streets.”

Garcia wrote a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in May demanding information on why Noem, the former DHS secretary, was still living in a Coast Guard residence months after Trump ousted her from the role.

House Democrats are seeking to use their oversight powers to scrutinize companies’ pricing practices and their role in driving up costs for consumers.

Garcia had sent a letter to Chris Rogers, the CEO of Instacart, last year requesting documents and information after a Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative, and More Perfect Union investigation found that Instacart used technology that charged shoppers different prices for the same products.

“At a time when families are struggling to put food on the table, it is unconscionable for companies to squeeze even more money out of people, especially if they’re doing so with secretive and predatory algorithms,” Garcia said in a statement at the time.

The issue is expected to draw bipartisan support on the panel.

Comer, for instance, opened an investigation this year into big companies’ use of artificial intelligence to facilitate surveillance pricing, in which companies set individualized prices for consumers based on their personal data.

A Democratic aide said any corporations using “their algorithms making things more expensive” could be subject to investigation next year.

Democrats could also revisit scrutiny of pharmaceutical manufacturers and oil and gas companies, including those involved in the takeover of Venezuela’s petroleum industries. But investigations alone would not ensure that companies suffer penalties. Those decisions would likely be left up to the Federal Trade Commission or the Justice Department.

articles.title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
articles.summary: Armed and in uniform, agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors to ask residents about their immigration status whether the...
articles.body:
Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found.

The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.

Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters.

"What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."

The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people , all of them green card holders , on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote.

As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections.

"HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."

Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities.

"In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident of initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.

In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering.

Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN , describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms , approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS."

One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand.

The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment.

For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters.

"It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University.

"And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that — because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."

A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear."

In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, " Target List ."

That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS.

In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.

DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters.

"Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally," said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ."

"There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden.

She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

articles.title: The Memo: Zelensky looks for way back from brink with Trump, to little avail
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky looks to be seeking a way back from the brink in his relationship with the U.S. — but he does not appear to be finding a receptive audience in President Trump. That leaves doubt and suspicion shrouding the path ahead — even as some in the GOP express dismay at Trump’s…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky looks to be seeking a way back from the brink in his relationship with the U.S. — but he does not appear to be finding a receptive audience in President Trump.

That leaves doubt and suspicion shrouding the path ahead — even as some in the GOP express dismay at Trump’s recent shift toward harsher treatment of Kyiv and positive language about Vladimir Putin’s Russia.

A Zelensky social media post on Tuesday said that he had spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about various “sensitive issues.”

He added: “We were very concrete and the conversation was positive. We shared the things we have to manage. And we will manage them, I’m sure of it.”

But there wasn’t that much evidence of such assurance from Washington.

Speaking with reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday afternoon, Trump belittled Ukraine’s chances of prevailing in the war sparked by Putin’s February 2022 invasion.

“Russia is a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that’s what they’ve done. They’ve taken a very large piece of land. And, you know, you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week. They just march forward,” Trump said.

Moments later he added that the Kremlin has “a lot of people to draw from. Ukraine does not have a lot of people to draw from, and it’s time to make a deal.”

Trump famously promised on the 2024 campaign trail that he could end the war on his first day back in the presidency. His failure appears to irk him, but his irritation has recently become fused with a desire to pin the blame for high diesel prices in the U.S. on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.

“We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve gotten nothing back other than high diesel,” Trump complained on Tuesday.

In fact, high U.S. fuel prices are almost universally considered to be primarily a consequence of the war on Iran that Trump launched, in conjunction with Israel, approximately eight months ago.

High prices are now weighing down GOP chances in the midterms. In opinion polls that measure voter sentiment about specific issues, Trump usually fares worst on inflation and the cost of living.

These intertwined problems have led to a head-spinning sequence of events in relation to Ukraine within the past two weeks.

Trump has, in swift succession, announced a diesel deal with Russia, undercutting the economic pressure on Moscow that Ukraine’s allies have sought to create; suggested Ukraine should get a new president; announced he would waive sanctions on Russia that were passed by Congress in memory of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.); and suggested he might meet with Putin and Chinese premier Xi Jinping — with Zelensky apparently frozen out — to discuss how to end the war.

There have been more opaque events too, the exact details of which are contested.

Most dramatically, the Ukrainians say they have faced restrictions in their use of a satellite system which is vital to the effectiveness of their drone program.

The issue has led to a spate of allegations and denials as to who, if anyone, slowed down the usage of a program known as Starshield, which is in effect a military off-shoot of the Elon Musk-owned Starlink.

Trump has denied he did so and has expressed skepticism that Musk would have, either. Musk has commented only obliquely, noting that Starshield is run by the Pentagon and that ultimate authority over it rests with the president.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday afternoon that it was Musk who had ordered the slowdown. The Journal also claimed, citing two sources, that “Musk and Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public.” One of those sources said that the two men had also discussed the matter prior to the slowdown.

Reuters had previously reported that the order to limit Starshield had come from “inside the White House.”

Separate from the Starshield issue, Kyiv has also leveled accusations that the U.S. had paused sharing of vital intelligence, leaving it in the dark about Russian ballistic missile launches. This has been denied by the U.S., most starkly by Rubio.

Speaking to reporters in Mumbai, India, on Tuesday Rubio insisted: “There has not been some deliberate, political directive to go out and harm Ukraine. It’s just not accurate.” He called the suggestion that Ukrainians had died because the U.S. had denied them information “scandalous” and “outrageous.”

Meanwhile, addressing Ukraine’s shortage of interceptor missiles, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters traveling with him in Wisconsin, “We haven’t changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well.”

Zelensky on Tuesday said that “early warning is now working.” He also referred to the importance of “our American partners” as he met Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff. The Ukrainian president wrote on social media that the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner had “joined us online.”

The exact specifics of what was discussed is unclear, though Zelensky made reference to the security guarantees that his nation has long sought, and to the idea of having a meeting with himself, Trump and Putin.

Trump’s overall stance has drawn criticism from some GOP lawmakers. Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who is retiring, told CNN ‘s Jake Tapper on Monday that comments from Trump playing down recent Russian attacks were “absolutely disgraceful” and that Trump was “morally blind” on the conflict.

Some experts have been similarly critical.

John Herbst, who served as U.S. ambassador to Ukraine during former President George W. Bush’s administration, told an Atlantic Council event on Tuesday that Trump was using “classic accommodationist tactics” and was engaged in “a truly misguided policy, which guarantees there’ll be no end to this war.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: GOP senators not happy about Trump’s warming relationship with Putin
articles.summary: President Trump’s warming relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which may lead to a trilateral summit of the United States, Russia and China to resolve the fate of Ukraine, is getting strong pushback from Republicans in Congress. Several Republicans have panned the idea that Trump would huddle with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, two…
articles.body:
President Trump’s warming relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which may lead to a trilateral summit of the United States, Russia and China to resolve the fate of Ukraine, is getting strong pushback from Republicans in Congress.

Several Republicans have panned the idea that Trump would huddle with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, two foreign leaders largely viewed in Congress as adversaries to American interests, to cut a peace deal that Ukraine would be forced to accept.

Trump told reporters this week at the White House he would be open to a trilateral summit with Putin and Xi but said the focus should be on nuclear weapons and nuclearization and possibly trade as well.

But the prospect Trump could also cut a deal on Ukraine with Russia and China is leaving some Republican senators alarmed after Trump surprised GOP lawmakers on Friday by issuing an executive order waiving tough new sanctions against Russia that Congress approved last month.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) called a potential summit with Putin and Xi to decide Ukraine’s fate “foolhardy” and “morally wrong.”

“To not include Ukraine is nonsense,” he told Sirius XM’s “The Julie Mason Show.”

“Ukrainians have got to be part of any peace deal. It’s not only essential because otherwise we won’t have peace, but it’s also the right thing to do,” he added. “Russia is trying to kill Americans around the world, covertly and overtly.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) declared in a CNN interview that “Putin is playing President Trump like a fiddle” and warned “history is not going to look good on an America that failed to rise up and defend the Western world if Putin actually gets his way.”

The North Carolina Republican warned that Xi and Putin “want to overwhelm the world” and dismissed the idea of a trilateral summit between the United States, Russia and China on striking a peace deal in Ukraine as “absurd.”

Daniel Fried, a former ambassador to Poland and former assistant secretary of State for European affairs for several administrations, said the proposal for a trilateral summit recalls the Yalta Conference toward the end of World War II, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin struck the deal to carve up postwar Europe into spheres of influence.

“A great power deal about [Ukraine] without them is called a new Yalta, and now you have the Russians proposing it. The Russians love it. The potential victims of such a deal hate it, and Republicans used to,” Fried said, noting Republicans for two generations decried the great-power dynamics of the Yalta Conference more than 80 years ago.

Fried noted some Republicans retain their traditional skepticism of the realpolitik approach taken by Trump, Putin and Xi.

“That muscle memory in the Republican Party is not entirely forgotten,” he said, calling the proposed summit “a terrible idea.”

“We would choose diplomatic ground stacked against us,” he warned. “We would be in a weaker position, and the idea that Trump is wary enough and nimble enough to avoid traps and blandishments is simply not credible.”

Fried, a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council who has served in the Clinton, Bush and Obama administrations, warned “if Ukraine was discussed, you could have Trump ending up in a bad or irreparably bad situation.”

Former Republican Sen. Judd Gregg (N.H.), who previously served as ranking member of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on State and Foreign Operations, called Trump’s decision to waive Russia sanctions that were included in legislation named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a strong Trump ally, “beyond inexcusable.”

“These sanctions were put in with his support, I presume, and they reflect a very strong opinion of the Congress and of the American people that Russia has invaded a democracy and killed tens of thousands of people and they are very clearly at fault,” he said.

“We should not be endorsing a dictatorship that has used power in this way to kill innocent people and to invade countries which they have no right to be in,” he added. “These sanctions … passed because there was legitimate and appropriate — and there continues to be legitimate and appropriate — outrage with the actions of Putin.”

Some Trump allies argue the president is simply keeping an open line of communication with powerful foreign rivals.

“Trump wants to always have some sort of relationship with his adversaries even if he’s doing a small deal so that when he really needs to push back and get something done, he can. He knows that Putin is a killer. He knows that Xi wants world domination,” said Ford O’Connell, a GOP strategist and former Trump campaign surrogate.

He added Trump is clear-eyed about whom he is dealing with in Putin and Xi.

But even some of Trump’s most loyal allies in the Senate think he’s giving Putin too much credibility.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) told The Hill last month that Trump’s invitation to Putin to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December was “giving Vladimir Putin more credit than he deserves.”

Trump’s decision to waive sanctions came a few days after Ukrainian officials blamed Washington for restricting its access to Starshield, the vital satellite-based internet network that enables Ukrainian forces to operate drones and other military aircraft to intercept Russian attacks.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Elon Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX, which owns Starlink and it’s military-focused sister company, Starshield, ordered the slowdown of Ukrainian access, citing people familiar with the matter.

The Journal reported Musk and Trump discussed the decision to limit Ukraine’s access to the network shortly after the slowdown of critical internet access became public.

Four Republican senators, Sens. John Cornyn (Texas), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Tillis, signed a bipartisan letter on Thursday to Platte Moring, the Defense Department’s inspector general, demanding an immediate investigation into whether senior Pentagon officials ordered or had advance knowledge of the Starshield slowdown.

The controversy over Starshield erupted in Washington a few days after Trump stunned GOP allies on Capitol Hill by announcing a deal with Putin to immediately import an estimated 2.2 million tons of Russian diesel into the United States to combat high fuel prices, which have hit farmers, truckers and business owners hard.

Senate Republican Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) said she was “surprised” by that announcement and said it raised questions about the Trump administration following the law and wishes of Congress.

She noted Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel only weeks after signing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which passed the Senate in August by an overwhelming vote of 86-11.

“I worry more that this is an act of Congress that we worked with the White House on and … we had timed this to when the president and the White House felt it was a good time to move forward with this, where it could be effective,” she said of the new sanctions law.

“I was extremely surprised when he did it,” she said of Trump’s deal to import hundreds of tons of Russian diesel without advance notification to Congress. “I worry about those dynamics … the legislative and executive.”

Trump made the deal weeks before the midterm elections, which have been dominated by voters’ concerns over high prices, including the price of diesel fuel. Trump has linked the higher diesel costs to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian fuel infrastructure, though the prices appear to be more of a result of the restricted Strait of Hormuz and the war with Iran.

The Wall Street Journal, which is part of the conservative-leaning Murdoch family’s media empire, criticized Trump for sticking “a shiv in the back of the legacy of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham,” who was an ardent advocate for tougher sanctions on Russia before dying of a heart issue in July.

articles.title: The next Senate class will decide Social Security’s fate. Can they meet halfway to save it?
articles.summary: The 2027 Senate class will be the first delegation in more than four decades forced to address Social Security’s potential insolvency. The federal program is poised to run out of funds by 2032, triggering a 22-percent cut in benefits for tens of millions of Americans unless lawmakers act. Some bipartisan consensus has emerged among Senate…
articles.body:
The 2027 Senate class will be the first delegation in more than four decades forced to address Social Security’s potential insolvency.

The federal program is poised to run out of funds by 2032 , triggering a 22-percent cut in benefits for tens of millions of Americans unless lawmakers act. Some bipartisan consensus has emerged among Senate hopefuls and incumbents locked in key battleground races in Iowa, Maine and New Hampshire this fall, but Congress is still racing against the clock.

“The longer we wait, the narrower the operating room becomes for the types of changes you can make,” said Andrew Eschtruth, director of the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College.

The looming depletion puts lawmakers in a politically tough spot as they weigh increasing taxes or cutting benefits. Social Security has largely taken a backseat on the campaign trail, with many candidates offering vague policy proposals and commitments, despite broad support for the program and its future.

Democratic lawmakers have proposed raising or eliminating the program’s payroll tax cap, raising the payroll tax rate and changing the cost-of-living adjustment to keep up with inflation. Republicans, meanwhile, have generally backed proposals like raising the retirement age and reducing or phasing out certain benefits for higher-income earners.

“It is challenging politically for Republicans to have a position on Social Security for the very reason that the administration has articulated a desire not to cut benefits” while also being opposed to raising taxes, Eschtruth explained. President Trump has vowed to defend the program.

More than 75 million Americans receive Social Security benefits, and 43 percent of seniors rely on the benefits as their main income, per AARP . The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget projects more than 60 million people would be impacted if the program’s trust fund runs out by 2032.

Ninety-five percent of Americans said they view Social Security as a critical program, while 91 percent said they want Congress to take action to preserve it, an August AARP poll shows.

The Social Security issue is particularly fraught in Maine, New Hampshire and Iowa. About 1 in 4 Mainers and New Hampshirites, and more than 1 in 5 Iowans receive Social Security payments, according to 2025 AARP data.

“Older Americans are a powerhouse in terms of voting in every state, and in every state that has a competitive Senate election, as we’ve been doing in our polling, we’ve shown that older voters are extremely motivated to vote, and they’re very focused on this issue,” said Bill Sweeney, senior vice president of government affairs at AARP.

All three Senate races could decide control of Congress. Iowa and Maine are rated as toss-ups by Decision Desk HQ, while New Hampshire leans toward Democrats.

The Hill surveyed the Senate campaigns for both parties in the three states. The Hill referred to previous remarks, including on the debate stage, as well as AARP candidate questionnaires for policy positions.

Democrats in two states — Iowa’s Josh Turek and Maine’s Troy Jackson — indicated they support either raising or eliminating the payroll tax cap. New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas, a Democrat, signaled he was also open to the move .

The payroll tax rate is 12.4 percent, and it is typically split evenly between an employer and a worker. The payroll taxes are capped at $184,500, meaning higher earners don’t pay additional taxes.

Increasing the cap to target higher earners is widely popular, a 2025 survey from the National Academy of Social Insurance, AARP, the National Institute on Retirement Security, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Greenwald Research found. Yet, the move wouldn’t be enough to fill the gap.

“When it comes to the tax increases, we certainly need to be thinking about asking for more from those who can most support it, but we can’t just rely on taxes on the rich to solve all of the spending needs that we have as a country,” said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center.

Privatization — diverting some portion of payroll taxes to a separate investment fund — has been mulled over by Republicans in the past. That option, however, poses more financial risk for everyday Americans.

Privatization and raising the retirement age were largely nonstarters for Democrats on the campaign trail — and for some Republicans. Another measure Republicans have previously floated is reducing or phasing out benefits for spouses and children of higher-earning Social Security recipients, which has garnered support among voters.

Republican Ashley Hinson of Iowa opposed raising the retirement age, which is also considered deeply unpopular among voters. She appeared supportive of creating a commission to evaluate solutions to address insolvency. Pappas and Turek, along with Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R), also expressed interest in the idea.

Collins suggested such a commission could potentially be led by former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-Utah). She has been receptive to adjusting the payroll tax cap as well.

Hinson is also opposed to partial or full privatization, her campaign told The Hill after the congresswoman suggested she’d be open to “separate investment funds” on the debate stage earlier this month. The campaign clarified Hinson meant lawmakers need to get creative about how to raise revenue within the broader Social Security trust fund.

New Hampshire’s Republican candidate for Senate, John E. Sununu, previously backed an opt-in option where Americans would be able to choose to put a portion of their payroll taxes into an investment fund. However, he has said that proposal is off the table this cycle. Sununu opposes any program provisions that would need to be continually renewed, and his campaign has called for “common-sense principles” to drive any future policy.

Social Security’s fate is a politically delicate issue, and tough decisions will have to be made. For Akabas, any discussion of policy proposals is a step in the right direction.

“What we need candidates to be doing is leaving options on the table,” Akabas said. “The more that both parties take aggressive positions against solutions that could be part of a bipartisan package, the harder it’s ultimately going to be to reach such an agreement.”
