articles.title: Vance could face 2028 challenge in addressing corruption
articles.summary: Vice President Vance’s role as President Trump’s chief defender poses a growing challenge as the administration faces mounting perceptions of inside dealing and corruption. Vance on Monday said the idea of Trump using the White House for personal enrichment was “laughable” and, during a CBS News town hall over the weekend, he said he doesn’t…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance’s role as President Trump’s chief defender poses a growing challenge as the administration faces mounting perceptions of inside dealing and corruption.

Vance on Monday said the idea of Trump using the White House for personal enrichment was “laughable” and, during a CBS News town hall over the weekend, he said he doesn’t see evidence of corruption. That puts him increasingly out of step with most voters, including an expanding segment of Republicans.

Six in 10 respondents to a recent Fox News survey said they were extremely concerned about government corruption, putting it ahead of other key issues like inflation and healthcare.

Nearly 2 in 3 Americans say Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, according to a new Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll. It found that most of the increase over the past year comes from Republicans and independents who lean Republican — a 12-point difference from September 2025.

“What else are you supposed to say?” one GOP strategist told The Hill. “Whether you do or you don’t, you’re still never going to say yes.”

“I see what the polls are saying, but the polls may change completely on this issue, and it’s an issue that bedevils both parties,” the strategist said.

Trump has seen a net worth increase since his win in 2024, as his family has made money from cryptocurrency ventures and his own stock trades .

Trump’s annual financial disclosure, released in late June, showed the president made more than $1 billion from his various crypto ventures last year.

Democrats have already vowed to investigate Trump and administration officials for corruption if they retake control of Congress.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) on social media wrote , “JD [Vance] – I’ve got 15 free minutes before my son’s hockey practice ends, so let me see how many of Trump’s enrichment schemes you didn’t see that I can remind you of,” followed by a list of ways Trump has made money off the presidency.

“Listen man, we get it,” Murphy wrote, still addressing the vice president. “If you work for Trump, you agree to lie and let your boss steal from taxpayers. But NO ONE believes you.”

Vance’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

“I think most people understand that Trump has made a substantial amount of money on ventures that the government regulates, and that people around him are making a substantial amount of money, whether it be family members or aides or ex-aides,” Arizona-based GOP strategist Barrett Marson said. “The money is free-flowing to people in or connected to the Trump administration. I’m not sure that you can deny that reality.”

Vance is “just trying to be a defender,” Marson said.

One national political consultant told The Hill that Vance’s comments “speak to a larger issue should he run for president.”

“Not necessarily his thoughts on corruption, but his inability to separate from Trump on virtually everything,” the national political consultant said. “[Former Vice President] Kamala Harris lost for a variety of reasons, but one of them was when she was on ‘The View’ when she was unable to offer any critique of the Biden administration. In what world is JD Vance allowed to say anything critical of President Trump?”

The unnamed GOP strategist argued that “every Republican who becomes the nominee — the Democrats are going to try to make them answer for Trump in every way, shape or form.”

Trump’s approval rating hit a record low in the Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll from over the weekend — 33 percent approval. It’s an 8-point difference from this time last year .

The national political consultant said that if a GOP candidate wants to win in 2028, they’re going to have to create separation “that doesn’t completely p— off Donald Trump.”

“I mean, if Trump continues to be this unpopular, they’re going to have no choice,” the political consultant noted.

But Marson said Vance might not have to talk about corruption.

“For someone like JD Vance, if he’s not involved, that’s for other people to answer,” Marson said. “If President Trump or a Cabinet secretary or an ambassador is doing something wrong, that’s something for them to answer to.”

He said that Vance, who chairs the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, could pivot and talk about his progress.

Vance has held meetings and roundtables with officials, including two press briefings, to highlight the fraud they’ve found. He also appeared Tuesday with Trump in the Oval Office to announce a $25 million whistleblower program that would pay money to those who tip off the government about fraudsters.

The GOP strategist agreed, saying, “The anti-fraud stuff really plays well for him, and he can say, ‘Hey, look, this is what I did.’”

images.caption: Vice President Vance listens as President Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 20, 2026, in Washington.

articles.title: Marshall, Hamilton set to take debate stage in tight Kansas Senate race
articles.summary: The top candidates in the Kansas Senate race will face off on the debate stage on Wednesday evening with less than two weeks until Election Day. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is fending off a challenge from Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton in a race that has grown increasingly competitive. The pair will face questions about…
articles.body:
The top candidates in the Kansas Senate race will face off on the debate stage on Wednesday evening with less than two weeks until Election Day.

Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is fending off a challenge from Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton in a race that has grown increasingly competitive.

The pair will face questions about issues like economic growth, infrastructure and healthcare during the event hosted by Nexstar Media Group, The Hill’s parent company. The debate will kick off at 7 p.m. in Kansas City, Mo. and run for one hour.

The race has tightened in recent weeks, eliciting concern among Republicans that Hamilton, a prominent pastor and moderate Democrat, could be successful in his effort to oust Marshall from his Senate seat.

Election handicappers, like Sabato’s Crystal Ball and The Cook Political Report , have shifted the race to a “toss up” amid the Democrat’s rise in the polls. Marshall and Hamilton were tied up in a New York Times survey conducted at the end of last month, with each candidate displaying narrow leads within the margin of error in other recent polls.

During a Sept. 12 debate at the Kansas State Fair hosted by local outlet KWCH 12 News, the two candidates sparred over the Trump administration’s tariffs and military operations against Iran.

The Republican incumbent faced jeers from the crowd during his answer to a question about the Iran war and a group of protesters shouted “shame on you” during his response to another question about how he handled unpaid medical bills when he was a doctor in a rural Kansas community.

Marshall has attacked Hamilton as a “megachurch pastor” and pointed to his sermons to claim that the Democratic candidate is “woke” on issues like gender and sexuality, climate change and the Black Lives Matter movement.

Kansas has historically elected Republican candidates to the U.S. Senate and White House. State voters have occasionally elected moderate Democrats to the governor’s office.

In 2024, President Trump won the Sunflower State by 16 points, but he has seen his approval ratings in the state waver amid rising nationwide discontent with his administration’s tariffs and rising costs amid the Iran war.

Trump stumped for Marshall on Monday evening at a rally in Wichita, Kansas, in which he used an antisemitic slur to defend the Republican incumbent for reports that he sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid medical bills.

“He was mandated by law to request, strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it, you have to by law go after those people,” the president said, before using a slur to describe how he felt the reporting characterized the candidate.

Hamilton said on Monday he was “glad” the president was campaigning for his opponent, telling CNN’s Jake Tapper he viewed Trump’s travel to Kansas as a “big compliment.”

“I took it as a statement that the Republican Party felt they needed to send the most powerful man in the country to try to save Roger Marshall, and I think it’s only going to hurt him,” Hamilton said, adding, “So I’m glad he’s here.”

articles.title: How Saudi Arabia's defense vulnerabilities could become Trump's problem amid Houthi onslaught
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia seeks foreign allies to counter Houthi missiles and drones as Trump weighs whether to launch direct U.S. military strikes on Yemen.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia is turning to foreign allies to fend off Houthi missiles and drones, exposing a military vulnerability that could soon become President Donald Trump's problem. Britain announced Tuesday it would send Typhoon fighter jets to defend Saudi cities and critical infrastructure. Egypt is already assisting the kingdom and Israel has offered to step in to help. Riyadh, meanwhile, is asking Washington for more interceptors, and Trump is weighing whether the U.S. should intervene and strike the Iran-backed Houthis directly. The reinforcements could help shield Saudi cities and critical infrastructure. They do little, however, to eliminate the Houthi launchers and weapons threatening them from Yemen. SAUDI FOREIGN MINISTER WARNS HOUTHI THREAT GOES GLOBAL AS TRUMP HOLDS FIRE "The theme right now, I think, is defensive or defensive-minded," Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital. The question, he said, is whether that evolves into something "more offensive or kinetic." The Houthis have already demonstrated their ability to punch through Saudi defenses. Their strikes and attempted strikes on the kingdom more than doubled in a single week this month, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, with airports in Riyadh, Jizan, Najran, Dammam and Abha targeted since Oct. 5. SAUDI ARABIA ON EDGE: ICONIC KINGDOM CENTRE SENDS WORKERS HOME AMID HOUTHI ATTACKS The most devastating barrage struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300. Other attacks have targeted Saudi energy infrastructure, turning the Houthi campaign into a threat not only to the kingdom's security but also to the economic stability Riyadh has spent years trying to project. Saudi Arabia has spent decades building one of the region's most sophisticated militaries. Riyadh spent an estimated $83.2 billion on defense last year, making it the eighth-largest military spender in the world, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Its arsenal includes U.S.-made F-15 fighter jets, Patriot missile defenses and advanced radar systems. Yet the Houthis are exploiting a mismatch between the defenses Saudi Arabia and its partners spent years building and the weapons now coming at them. Campbell said the U.S. and its regional partners had been comparatively well-prepared to confront the higher end of Iran's arsenal, including ballistic missiles and other advanced weapons. PENTAGON RACES TO BUY 10X MORE MISSILES AS IRAN WAR DWINDLES ARSENAL, THREATENS READINESS FOR CHINA AGGRESSION "What the region was decidedly less prepared for was an array of lower end of the spectrum ... threats posed by Iran and now the Houthis," Campbell said. The volume is part of the problem. Campbell said Saudi Arabia and other U.S. partners have burned through significant numbers of high-end interceptors against ballistic missiles and other threats, while lower-flying weapons can also challenge radar and early-warning systems that were not necessarily designed or calibrated to detect them. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Riyadh is competing with allies around the world — and the U.S. military itself — for a limited supply of the interceptors needed to defend against missile attacks. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today; they’d like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling them "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field." The U.S. cannot meet every request, Rubio acknowledged. American forces must maintain minimum air-defense requirements at bases around the world, while the sophisticated interceptors are expensive and take time to manufacture even as production increases. "We have our own needs too," Rubio said. Saudi Arabia's sheer size compounds the challenge. The kingdom stretches across more than 800,000 square miles, leaving cities, airports, oil facilities and military installations spread across a vast territory. "Saudi Arabia is a huge geography to protect, and this speaks to a larger threat we’re facing globally: a relatively small nonstate actor can pose a serious challenge to even a sophisticated and extremely expensive military," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, told Fox News Digital. "The Houthis can impose enormous costs without having to spend very much themselves." That imbalance helps explain why Saudi Arabia is increasingly looking beyond its own military for protection. But outside assistance may have limits. "Many years later, everyone is realizing that the Houthis are not just Saudi Arabia’s problem, but everyone’s problem — whether that’s Turkey, Egypt, France, the UK or others," Al-Muslimi said. "But I don’t think this outside support will make a significant military difference unless the U.S. is directly involved." That leaves Trump facing a potentially consequential decision: whether to continue helping Saudi Arabia defend against incoming attacks or go further and target the Houthis directly. Trump has kept direct U.S. military action on the table. Asked earlier this month whether the U.S. could join Saudi strikes against the Houthis, he said, "We may. We’re gonna look at it." "We’ll make a decision," Trump said. "We move very quickly." But direct U.S. intervention would not be without precedent — or questions about what another bombing campaign could accomplish. Operation Rough Rider targeted Houthi positions across Yemen for roughly two months in 2025 before Trump halted the operation after Oman brokered an agreement with the group. "We’ve already seen the U.S. conduct a 60-day bombing campaign of Houthi strongholds in Yemen with limited, if any, real strategic benefits," Campbell said. A new campaign would also compete for U.S. military resources amid the war with Iran. Campbell said taking on the Houthis would require clearer objectives and likely contributions from a broader coalition. Israel has also offered to help defend Saudi Arabia, an offer Trump has publicly encouraged Riyadh to accept. But bringing Israel openly into the fight could create a different problem for the kingdom. "If I were Saudi, I would never accept help like that," Al-Muslimi said. "The optics are enormously difficult. Saudi Arabia is the custodian of the two holiest mosques in Islam, and appearing alongside Netanyahu to fight another Yemeni group would be a nonstarter for much of Saudi society." For now, the U.S. continues to provide intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia as its allies focus on defending the kingdom. "The collective effort seems to be at stemming the threat to the Saudi kingdom itself," Campbell said. But as Al-Muslimi cautioned, even a stronger defensive coalition may not eliminate the danger. "It can make Saudi Arabia safer, but it doesn’t solve the larger problem of dismantling the Houthi threat." The latest fighting is another chapter in a war that has torn through Yemen for more than a decade. The Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military intervention the following year against the Iran-backed group and in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Years of Saudi airstrikes failed to dislodge the Houthis, while the group steadily expanded its missile and drone capabilities with support from Tehran. The conflict eventually settled into an uneasy truce before erupting again this year, with Saudi-backed forces fighting Houthi advances on the ground and the Houthis increasingly taking the war across the border into Saudi Arabia. Yemeni civilians are again bearing much of the cost. More than 250,000 people have fled the renewed fighting, according to the United Nations. WHO recorded at least 674 deaths and nearly 3,000 injuries in just six weeks of fighting between August and September, while millions were already facing severe hunger and displacement after more than a decade of war.

articles.title: Marshall faces final debate in fight for political life
articles.summary: In today’s issue: Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) faces his second and final debate against Democrat Adam Hamilton as the first-term Republican fights for his political life in a razor-tight race. The race has the potential to be biggest surprise of the entire midterm cycle, in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since the…
articles.body:
Marshall, Hamilton meeting in final debate

Trump unveils fraud whistleblower program

Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) faces his second and final debate against Democrat Adam Hamilton as the first-term Republican fights for his political life in a razor-tight race.

The race has the potential to be biggest surprise of the entire midterm cycle, in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since the 1930s. Polling has shown the race to be essentially dead even, as Hamilton leads in the Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) polling average by 0.4 points.

Tonight’s debate, hosted by Nexstar Media Group affiliate WDAF, will air at 7 p.m. CDT and run for one hour. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

Marshall started out the race as the heavy favorite , with DDHQ giving him as high as a 90 percent chance of winning this summer, but that now sits at just 65 percent, making him one of the most vulnerable Senate Republican incumbents this cycle.

Democrats have found some recent success in the state’s gubernatorial races behind popular moderate Gov. Laura Kelly (D). But a Democrat hasn’t won another statewide office in Kansas in decades, and Republicans have mostly dominated the U.S. House delegation for more than a century.

Hamilton, a prominent pastor who has leaned into his Kansas roots, is trying to change their fortunes.

He’s sought to tie Marshall to President Trump as the president’s approval rating has dipped. An Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media survey conducted last month found Trump’s approval rating in the state stood at 40 percent, while 53 percent of respondents said they disapproved of his job performance.

Hamilton has torn into Marshall over the Iran war and his refusal to support war powers resolutions in the Senate to limit Trump’s authority. He’s also seized on a New York Times report that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills, including 81 who were arrested, during his time working as an obstetrician-gynecologist.

A spokesperson for Marshall told the Times that he spent decades caring for patients regardless of their ability to pay and that judges issue arrest warrants for missed court dates, not doctors.

But that hasn’t stopped Hamilton from seizing on the report, releasing an ad featuring one woman who was arrested.

Viewers can expect more of these attacks from Hamilton tonight.

There have been several internal and external signs that Republicans have reason for concern.

Election handicappers Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both shifted their ratings of the race from “Lean Republican” to “Toss-up” this month.

The Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC that works to elect Republicans to the Senate, is investing $14 million to boost Marshall after having pulled out of North Carolina, a seat that Democrats seem likely to flip.

Trump made a stop in Kansas to campaign for Marshall on Monday, announcing an $8 billion program to provide relief to farmers dealing with high diesel costs. He credited Marshall with pushing for the program and went after Hamilton, accusing him of “pretending to be a moderate.”

Hamilton has said he would be independent-minded and willing to break with his own party if elected.

Marshall has tried to label Hamilton as “woke,” pointing to sermons he’s given on issues like gender and sexuality and climate change.

But even Marshall has sought to distance himself from Trump on a few issues, pushing back last month when the president floated banning sales of the Canadian private jet maker Bombardier in the U.S. The company has a large workforce in Kansas. He also called on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to work more closely with local police departments during a sudden sweep the agency conducted in the state.

How closely Marshall hugs Trump’s positions or shows willingness to break with him will be a key aspect to watch on the debate stage.

“I took it as a statement that the Republican Party felt they needed to send the most powerful man in the country to try to save Roger Marshall,” Hamilton said on CNN in response to Trump’s visit. “And I think it’s only going to hurt him.”

Russia has released Stephen Hubbard , a retired American teacher, from custody four years after he was taken in 2022 as Russia swept through Ukrainian territory at the outset of its full-scale invasion, special envoy Steve Witkoff announced during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The U.S. had considered Hubbard to be wrongfully detained.

Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starshield , the military version of Starlink, hampering Ukraine’s defenses in the war against Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported. Musk initially said only Trump or the military could order the slowdown, noting the SpaceX software is owned by the U.S. government.

Democratic Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.) and Robert Garcia (Calif.) are the latest public figures to receive suspicious packages at their offices ahead of the midterms. Law enforcement sources told ABC News that more than 100 letters with white powder are apparently circulating in the U.S. mail system.

WHISTLEBLOWERS WELCOME: Trump and Vice President Vance announced a $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program that would give monetary rewards to people who provide tips to the federal government that lead to a successful conviction.

“If anybody turns anybody in… you get a 1 percent commission, and I think that will be amazing, because the kind of money that’s been stolen is trillions from this country,” Trump said in the Oval Office.

Trump said he will act as the sole arbiter of who receives payouts, and if there are multiple claims to the same reward, Trump said he would intervene to “expedite” the process. Anyone can submit a tip through fraud.gov, Trump said.

Conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley — who posted videos documenting his search for fraudulent childcare programs in Minnesota last year — joined the president and vice president in the Oval Office yesterday. He will apparently become the first person to receive a reward through the program, with Fox News reporting he is set to receive $10,000.

The program is meant to build on Vance’s work as chair of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, which Trump created in March with the goal of looking into and reducing fraud in federal government programs.

▪ NPR : Fraud, Trump policies drive friction in Minnesota Senate debate.

UKRAINE TALKS : U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday amid fraying relations between the two countries as Trump appears to soften toward Russia in the weeks leading up to the election.

The talks took place in Oslo, Norway, and included leaders from both Norway and Finland. Kushner attended the meeting virtually.

A White House official told NewsNation that the meeting’s objective was to “continue aligning on a comprehensive proposal that can form the basis for renewed negotiations with Russia.” They said Witkoff would plan to next travel to Russia to meet with Putin and present ideas developed with Ukrainian and European partners.

▪ The Hill : Pete Hegseth says U.S. approach to Ukraine unchanged.

FBI PROBE: The FBI investigated whether two of the biggest names in South Carolina — the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R) and Rep. James Clyburn (D) — were involved in a bribery scheme connected to Hawaiian naval defense contractor Navatek, according to a report published by ProPublica .

The report says Navatek CEO Martin Kao told the FBI that Graham agreed to grant a $10 million government contract to the company in South Carolina, allegedly in exchange for a pledge of $100,000 to Graham’s reelection campaign.

The contractor made similar deals with Clyburn and Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) after approaching their offices in 2019, according to the report.

ProPublica previously reported that Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) had been investigated by the FBI for allegedly steering funding toward Navatek after Kao made illegal donations to her campaign. Collins has strongly denied the allegations and denounced Kao as a “convicted liar.”

The investigation into lawmakers on both sides of the aisle effectively ended when the team looking into it was gutted once Trump came back into office.

▪ KGO : FBI agent details alleged corruption of former Oakland mayor at trial.

MIDTERM SPENDING : Money is pouring into the midterm races, with less than two weeks to go before Election Day.

Trump announced on Truth Social yesterday that he will be spending a total of more than $400 million on the midterms, including the more than $300 million that’s “already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more.”

The Republican National Committee is also spending more than $50 million on House and Senate races in the final two weeks before Election Day, The New York Times reported.

And former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg (D) announced plans to spend $80 million to boost Democrats in competitive midterm races throughout the country.

The president will participate in a roundtable at 2:30 p.m. He will travel to Clemson, S.C., to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. and then return to Washington.

DEFENDER-IN-CHIEF : The vice president’s role as Trump’s top defender could create a challenge for him as he considers a 2028 presidential bid.

Vance gained attention Monday after he brushed off the idea that Trump is using the White House for personal enrichment as “laughable.” He also said at a CBS town hall over the weekend that he doesn’t see any evidence of Trump enriching himself in office.

The Hill’s Mallory Wilson reports that puts Vance out of step with most voters. A Fox News poll found 6 in 10 respondents said they were extremely concerned about government corruption, while two-thirds said in a Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll that Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself.

“What else are you supposed to say?” one GOP strategist told The Hill of Vance’s remarks. “Whether you do or you don’t, you’re still never going to say yes.”

One national political consultant said the instance ties into a larger issue about Vance’s inability to separate himself from the president.

“[Former Vice President] Kamala Harris lost for a variety of reasons, but one of them was when she was on ‘The View’ when she was unable to offer any critique of the Biden administration. In what world is JD Vance allowed to say anything critical of President Trump?” the political consultant said.

Trump’s net worth has increased substantially since he won back the presidency in 2024, as his family has made money from cryptocurrency and his own stock trades. Democrats have vowed to investigate Trump and members of his administration if they win back control of Congress.

▪ The Hill : Trump deflects on possible Vance endorsement.

UGLY ATTACKS: Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton is fighting back against an ad from her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy that features her estranged mother accusing her of being a “liar” and telling Ohioans not to vote for her in November.

The ad gained visibility online Monday night after first appearing in a post by an Ohio political blogger but didn’t make clear who was behind it.

Acton was quick to accuse her opponent of being behind the ad, pointing to similar accusations he faced of running personal attacks when he ran for president. Ramaswamy later acknowledged that his campaign produced the ad , which a spokesperson said will air both online and on TV.

“This is a lifelong pattern with my opponent,” Acton told Spectrum News in an interview.

Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur , suggested in the ad that the Democrat has misrepresented her opponent and pushed back on Acton’s account of living in a tent with her family at one point during her childhood. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns , has backed up his sister’s account.

Acton has not seen her mother since she was 12 years old, when she and Stearns were removed from their mother’s custody after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child, according to a statement from her campaign. Arthur reportedly defended her husband in court.

Acton’s campaign also released its own ad later Tuesday featuring Stearns talking about their childhood abuse and accusing Ramaswamy of being behind the ad featuring their mother.

“She was 11 and 12 years old, and to think that that’s somehow a talking point. Shame on Vivek. It’s the contempt he has for Amy. It’s the contempt he has for Ohio. He’s not fit to lead,” Stearns said in the ad .

Republicans raised $1.2 billion to reach young voters. Democrats must respond , Celinda Lake and Eve Levenson write in The Hill.

Why everyone wants to meet with Kim Jong Un , Ruth Pollard writes in Bloomberg.

And finally … Prince Harry said a reconciliation with his family is the “most important thing” to him following his return to the United Kingdom.

The Duke of Sussex told GQ in an interview published Tuesday that he grieves the current relationship he has with his father, King Charles III , and brother, Prince William . He has reportedly been estranged from much of his family for years, but he and his wife, Meghan , the Duchess of Sussex, returned to the U.K. in August after spending six years in California.

“With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile,” he said.

articles.title: The false promise of free health care comes with an invoice for the middle class
articles.summary: “Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!” That’s the rally chant of Abdul El-Sayed, who won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August. It’s catchy. articles.body:
“Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!” That’s the rally chant of Abdul El-Sayed , who won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August.

It’s catchy. So was “If you like your health care plan, you can keep it.” PolitiFact named that line its 2013 Lie of the Year , but only after roughly 4 million Americans received cancellation notices due to ObamaCare.

El-Sayed has company. Minnesota’s Senate nominee, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, is campaigning on Medicare for All , and 102 House members joined Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) as cosponsors of her bill . The pitch goes like this: free care, coverage for everyone living here regardless of immigration status, and the tax bill gets mailed to somebody else.

I have spent more than 30 years in private equity, private credit and family offices reading pro formas. A projection that only works if you ignore the expense line is a dud — the middle class always ends up writing the check.

Start with that last promise. President Barack Obama said his plan would cut a typical family’s premium “by up to $2,500 a year.” PolitiFact has since rated it “Promise Broken .” Premiums rose so far that Congress had to tack on “enhanced” subsidies to them during COVID — one subsidy added on top of the original subsidy, just to make premiums slightly less intolerable. When those credits expired at the end of 2025 , the average monthly net premium jumped by 58 percent and the average deductible hit a record $3,786. Sixteen years in, the Affordable Care Act still can’t live up to its own name.

Democrats want the temporary credits made permanent — a move the Congressional Budget Office priced at $350 billion over a decade . What would that mean? Hospitals would charge exactly what they charge now (with prices rising over time). Your premium statement would look friendlier each month. The difference would land on a Treasury already carrying more than $40.3 trillion in debt . That is called refinancing a bad loan with a bigger bad loan — a fiscal doubling down on stupid.

Then comes the main event. The Medicare for All Act of 2025 says that “every individual who is a resident of the United States” is entitled to benefits. It bars discrimination based on “citizenship status.” The same bill makes it unlawful for a private insurer to sell coverage that duplicates the government plan. So you can keep your plan, right up until it becomes contraband. Your solid benefits package — perhaps even negotiated by your union in lieu of higher pay — would become illegal.

The price of Medicare for All runs into the trillions each year. The Congressional Budget Office studied five illustrative single-payer designs and found federal health subsidies would rise by $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion in 2030 alone . Its follow-up work found that paying for it with income or payroll taxes would leave GDP between 1 percent and 10 percent lower by 2030. It also warned that demand would outrun supply and produce “increased congestion.” After all, nobody conjures an extra hospital bed or a night-shift nurse by printing “free” on an insurance card.

Candidates insist the rich will pay. But the top 1 percent already paid 38.4 percent of federal income taxes in 2023 while earning only 20.6 percent of adjusted gross income; the bottom half paid 3.3 percent. Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) millionaires surtax would raise no more than $1.5 trillion over ten years .

Sen. Bernie Sanders’ billionaire wealth tax scores between $2.3 trillion and $4.4 trillion over a decade, and he has already spent every dime on paper — on $3,000 checks, a rollback of last year’s Medicaid and ACA changes and new Medicare dental coverage. Even if Sanders tore up his wish list, both bills together might cover two years of single-payer health care at the Congressional Budget Office’s high estimate. After that, the tax collector comes for payroll. Margaret Thatcher saw it in 1976: Socialist governments “ always run out of other people’s money .”

California offers a preview of Medicare for All. Sacramento extended full Medi-Cal (the state’s Medicaid program) to adults regardless of immigration status, then discovered it was spending about $8.5 billion a year from the general fund on that population, with costs running $2.7 billion over projections. The state then froze new enrollments for most non-citizen adults on Jan. 1, 2026 and announced it will be scaling back coverage for those already on the program. Routine dental was cut in July, and $30 monthly premiums will be required starting in 2027.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) is hardly a deficit hawk. When he slams the brakes on a program, you know it is unsustainable. It means that candidates promising the national version of this debacle are just selling oceanfront property in Arizona.

Currently, only 49 percent of adults rate as “cost secure” in the West Health-Gallup index , the lowest reading since it began in 2021. That is the proponents’ strongest argument. But a price problem calls for more supply and more competition, something Medicare for All cannot do.

Congress already made bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans eligible for Health Savings Accounts this year, opening tax-free accounts to about 7.3 million new enrollees. That’s the place to start. Next, raise the contribution limits. Enforce hospital price transparency with penalties that sting. Fund more residency slots, since the American Association of Medical Colleges projects a shortfall of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036 . Drive prices down, and coverage gets cheaper for everyone.

Before you vote on Nov. 3, you should put three questions to every candidate who supports Medicare for All. First, what tax rate hits my paycheck? Second, who is eligible? Third, how long will I wait for a specialist?

Channel your inner Jerry Maguire and make them show you the money. A candidate cannot answer those questions is handing you a pitch deck with no financials — a huge red flag that has prompted me to walk away from much better deals than this one.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: Evacuation and shelter-in-place orders after chemical release in North Toledo
articles.summary: Residents in north Toledo are being ordered to shelter-in-place or evacuate depending on their location after a chemical was released into the air late Tuesday night.
articles.body:
TOLEDO, Ohio (WJW) — Residents in north Toledo are being ordered to shelter-in-place or evacuate depending on their location after a chemical was released into the air late Tuesday night.

According to the City of Toledo website , at 10:48 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 20, Toledo Fire & Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1050 Progress Avenue to evacuate because of a hazardous materials release. At 4:24 a.m. on Wednesday, everyone within a 3-mile radius was advised to shelter in place.

The city didn’t immediately provide details of what chemical had been released into the air but described is as an irritant that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth, and skin.

“Symptoms of overexposure include headache, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting. Please contact a medical professional if you believe you’re having a reaction to exposure,” stated the city.

Complicating the situation, officials report dense fog in the Toledo area making it difficult to tell what is fog and what is a chemical plume.

“Please don’t rely on how the air looks,” stated the city alert.

Evacuees are being taken to temporary shelters at a nearby elementary school and a Meijer parking lot where Red Cross and public transit buses are stationed as temporary shelters.

Residents can find the latest updates, HERE .

*Vince Fratiani contributed to this report*

articles.title: Why judges are growing more skeptical of Trump’s Justice Department
articles.summary: A federal judge pressed Department of Justice (DOJ) lawyers this week on whether she should believe them or President Trump when it comes to the administration’s plans for a golf course in the nation’s capital. “I don’t know what to do when I keep getting different stories from the government,” U.S. District Judge Ana…
articles.body:
A federal judge pressed Department of Justice (DOJ) lawyers this week on whether she should believe them or President Trump when it comes to the administration’s plans for a golf course in the nation’s capital.

“I don’t know what to do when I keep getting different stories from the government,” U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes , an appointee of former President Biden , said during a contentious hearing Monday regarding the future of East Potomac Park.

The dispute exemplifies a broader pattern of judges taking a more skeptical approach to evaluating the government’s claims as Trump’s second term nears the halfway point.

It wasn’t the first time Reyes made her frustration known in the case, which pits preservationist groups against the government. During an emergency hearing on Oct. 12, she told DOJ attorneys that all credibility had been lost by not providing enough notice before hundreds of trees were chopped down in the park.

In turn, the DOJ accused her of violating “basic norms” of fairness and impartiality and insisted she recuse. Trump also attacked her on social media as a “crazed lunatic,” but Reyes did not relent.

The judge’s order refusing to step aside landed just hours before Trump claimed that his Interior Department did not need approval to move forward with a major renovation. He wrote Monday morning on Truth Social that work would start “IMMEDIATELY” — a timeline DOJ lawyers would later tell Reyes had not actually been finalized. The tension in the courtroom was palpable from the start Monday.

Just minutes into the hearing, Reyes ordered the DOJ to refile a brief asserting its position that the administration’s golf course plan was not ripe for review because “no final agency action” had been taken.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward was the only name on that filing, and Reyes demanded to know which other line attorneys were willing to sign on.

“Raise your hand if you’re willing to sign it,” the judge instructed the table of DOJ lawyers.

“[That’s] not an appropriate ask,” Woodward shot back.

“I’m the one who’s going to say how we move today,” Reyes said.

“You’re putting them in an incredibly untenable situation,” Woodward added.

The judge later withdrew that order after consulting clerks during a recess but cautioned that it was more difficult for her to have “confidence” in the DOJ’s filings when line attorneys are not on it.

But some see the decision to have politically appointed lawyers sign solo onto briefs as a way to insulate career lawyers from bearing the brunt of criticism in sensitive or controversial cases.

“For those wondering, a common reason high level DOJ appointees sometimes signs briefs boils down to good leadership,” Abhi Kambli , a former DOJ official in the Trump administration, wrote on social platform X . “If there is something that is likely to be contentious with a judge, a DOJ leader signs their name on the brief so that any issues someone has with the brief is directed at them rather than lower level attorneys.”

The testy exchanges did not stop between Reyes and the lawyers tasked with defending the administration against a lawsuit challenging the plans for East Potomac Park.

When lawyers claimed that there was “no final agency action” warranting the court’s intervention and no definitive plans to close the course next month for renovations, the judge questioned whom she should trust.

“Do I believe the president of the United States, or do I believe you?” she asked, referencing a Truth Social post from the day before in which Trump said the course would close on Nov. 15 for 15 months.

And Reyes is not alone. Judges across the country are looking at the government’s words more closely, and some are no longer giving them the benefit of the doubt.

As U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis , an appointee of former President Obama , put it last July in a case involving the Trump administration’s efforts to again deport Kilmar Ábrego Garcia : “You have taken the presumption of regularity and you have destroyed it.”

The legal principle generally rests on the idea that the government is acting honestly and in good faith. Its roots in Supreme Court jurisprudence trace back to an 1816 opinion, in which Justice Thomas Todd wrote that it should be presumed that “public officers act correctly until the contrary be shown.”

A study published by Just Security in March found that many judges have become less willing to take the government at face value during the second Trump administration. It pointed to a warning from U.S. District Judge Paul Friedman , an appointee of former President Clinton , in August 2025 that the president “may have forfeited the right to such a presumption of regularity.”

The authors counted 90 cases in which courts identified “serious defects in the government’s explanations and representations” since Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025, along with at least 35 other instances in habeas immigration cases.

Reyes is expected to rule soon on whether to extend an order that blocked the Trump administration from conducting any more tree removal work in East Potomac Park while the litigation plays out.

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams . Mahmoud Khalil heads to SCOTUS: The Columbia University graduate who spent months in immigration detention last year is taking his deportation fight to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to reverse an appeals court ruling that found a federal judge had no power to order his release from jail. Mahmoud Khalil has long argued that he was targeted by the Trump administration because of his participating in pro-Palestinian campus protests.

Musk settles: Billionaire Elon Musk has agreed to settle two lawsuits alleging that his America PAC defrauded battleground state voters by pledging to hand out $1 million checks ahead of the 2024 election.

Executive privilege invoked in Kennedy Center fight: The White House is asserting executive privilege to block the release of records of President Trump’s communications in an ongoing lawsuit from Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the future of the Kennedy Center.

Brennan suit axed: A federal judge in Washington, D.C., has tossed a lawsuit from former CIA Director John Brennan, ruling that he did not yet have standing. Brennan sought a court order that would force the Trump administration to preserve records related to ongoing federal investigations into his role reviewing foreign interference in the 2016 election.

Trump officials hit with Hatch Act complaint: Three Trump administration officials — Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick— are facing a Hatch Act complaint for participating in a mid-October campaign event for Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), who is seeking reelection.

What’s it like to win the SCOTUS lottery?: The Supreme Court rejects the vast majority of requests to hear cases, so it’s a lucky day for any advocate when their petition is granted. We appreciated the candid reaction from Pacific Legal Foundation’s Chris Kieser, who wrote on social media , “Holy crap I’m going to SCOTUS,” 10 minutes after learning his case was taken up.

Enjoy it while it lasts, Mr. Chief Justice: One of Trump’s new judicial nominees clerked for Chief Justice John Roberts. The president didn’t hesitate to highlight the connection in his Truth Social announcement, even calling Roberts “esteemed” after repeated public criticisms of him.

Judge allegedly abandoned post: Dallas-based U.S. District Judge Ada Brown’s colleagues have suspended her from hearing new cases over concerns about a “mental condition,” according to a newly unsealed order . It accuses Brown, a Trump appointee who serves in the Northern District of Texas, of failing to manage her docket, hurling racist insults and engaging in “hostile treatment.” Brown isn’t the only judge facing suspension, but at 51, she’s much younger than the 98-year-old jurist at the center of the other fight.

A cybersecurity incident has ensnared federal bankruptcy courts.

It’s impacting government contractor BAE Systems, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts.

BAE operates the systems that send out electronic bankruptcy notices for creditors and other interested parties. For days, the systems have been offline.

“The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts has been in communication with the impacted courts and is also coordinating with BAE Systems,” the office said in a statement. “BAE is actively investigating this incident and working to restore operations.”

It’s left bankruptcy judges grappling with how to move cases forward.

In the Eastern District of Texas, Chief Bankruptcy Judge Brenda Rhoades has extended the automatic pause on pending litigation that kicks in when someone files for bankruptcy.

In the Southern District of New York, Chief Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane guaranteed that “ no party shall be prejudiced ” by the interruption and signaled that parties should ask their judge if they need help.

“Upon request of a party in interest, or on its own initiative where permitted by law, the Court may extend or reset deadlines or continue hearings as necessary to address the interruption. Parties may request relief by written motion or orally at a previously scheduled hearing,” Lane wrote.

It’s the latest cybersecurity incident to hit the courts.

Last year, the federal judiciary’s electronic case filing system faced escalating cyberattacks, prompting efforts to enhance security .

And this summer, Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Elena Kagan told lawmakers they needed millions more in funding to counter the rise of artificial intelligence and shore up vulnerabilities in the Supreme Court’s digital system.

“Cybersecurity attacks have been up by magnitudes year after year,” Barrett testified. “We haven’t suffered the kind of paralyzing attacks that some of the lower courts have, but in seeing that, that has caused us to try to ramp up very quickly.”

Cases the Supreme Court is taking up — or passing on — this term.

The Supreme Court took up two of the petitions on our watchlist last week.

In Department of Justice v. McNutt , the justices will decide if a 160-year-old federal ban on distilling spirits at home is constitutional.

Congress has taxed liquor since the founding, and the government says the ban ensures people can’t avoid those taxes by putting their operation where officials can’t see it.

The Supreme Court will decide if it exceeds Congress’s constitutional authority to pass “necessary and proper” measures to carry out its powers.

The second case, Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, is the latest battle over the role of race in school admissions.

The justices will review the lottery-based system used by Montgomery County, Md., to admit students to its competitive middle schools.

It’s a key test of the Supreme Court’s decision invalidating affirmative action in higher education.

Montgomery County’s lottery is race-blind, but a group of Asian American parents say it has led to discrimination against their children under the guise of promoting diversity.

The court will decide the proper evidentiary standard for such lawsuits, which have also emerged in places like Northern Virginia and Boston.

OUT: Chicago parking enforcement challenge

Liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor and conservative Justice Neil Gorsuch teamed up a second time in as many weeks.

This time, the battle concerned Chicago’s parking enforcement system, which allows officials in some circumstances to sell people’s cars after they’ve accumulated debt from tickets.

A lower court rejected arguments that the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause applies. It requires the government to provide compensation when taking private property for public use. The lower court said the state police power is immune from that requirement.

“I have serious concerns about that conclusion,” Sotomayor wrote, joined by Gorsuch.

However, they agreed with their colleagues to turn away the Chicago parking battle, saying it wasn’t the right case to decide the issue, and it should percolate more in other lower courts.

The duo similarly teamed up last week to raise double jeopardy concerns about a Mexican man’s prosecution.

The Supreme Court asked the Trump administration for input on Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, the federal preemption battle over Iowa’s immigration law we previewed last month.

The court often goes with the sitting administration’s eventual recommendation about whether it should take up a case, though it often takes several months to come in.

Iowa wants the justices to reverse a ruling that it can’t pass a law making illegal immigration a state crime.

It’s one of multiple Republican-controlled states that have passed similar legislation, often in response to what they saw as inaction at the federal level by then- President Biden .

articles.title: Is Trump a RINO?
articles.summary: True conservatives are realizing that Trump is using the Republican Party for his own convenience.
articles.body:
One of President Trump’s most frequent and favorite epithets for his Republican antagonists is “RINO” — that is, “Republican in name only.” But the evidence suggests that the president should be mindful of the old adage: “People who live in glass houses should not throw stones.”

Nearing the midpoint of his second term, Trump has turned his back on long held Republican principles which have glued together the conservative movement for decades. This is very different from his first term, when he used his business acumen to produce solid economic growth through tax cuts and deregulation.

In February 2020, Trump’s approval rating stood at 49 percent and reelection prospects looked good. That was when COVID severely disrupted to everyday life and its economic wreckage soured voters on the party in charge.

Four years later, Trump put his name into the history books alongside that of Grover Cleveland, the only other president to serve two non-consecutive terms . But from the start of his second term, Trump pursued his publicly announced revenge agenda and allowed his insatiable ego to drive policy decisions aimed to please only his MAGA base.

Thus, there was no overriding governing philosophy. The principles of conservatism were left on the cutting room floor as the self-proclaimed “ very stable genius ” mode of operation became focused on the accumulation of power to the executive. Damn the courts! Full speed ahead.

Trump routinely attacks judges who issue a decision he does not like, throwing on the trash heap of governance our constitutional doctrine that the federal government consists of three co-equal branches. Even judges appointed by Trump himself are not exempt from his late-night tantrums on Truth Social. Ask Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

Starting trade wars with multiple longtime allies is nowhere to be found in previous Republican Party platforms. Trump’s renewed spite for Canada may end up costing Republicans control of the Senate as voters in Michigan and Maine take out their frustration by voting for clearly inferior Democratic Senate candidates . Perhaps Trump will explain why he did not wait until after the midterm election to economically attack America’s neighbor and longtime ally.

America’s commitment to freedom lies in tatters as Trump has weakened our commitment to NATO and cozies up to the murderous dictator Putin, even inviting him to the G20 meeting at Trump’s Doral Country Club. Now Trump wants to fund Putin’s war machine in exchange for diesel fuel , which is in short supply and now comes at an exorbitant cost. How many innocent Ukrainian civilians will die as a direct result of Trump’s ill-planned attack on Iran? May Lindsey Graham’s Russian sanctions legacy rest in peace .

Those actions are a very long way from “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.”

America’s level of debt is beyond comprehension. Six years of Trump and four years of Biden has taken America’s debt from $20 trillion to $40 trillion with more than half of that increase on Trump’s watch. There was a time when conservatives were opposed to increasing the debt.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget tells us that when the Social Security fund hits zero in 2032, current law requires a reduction in benefits of 24 percent for every senior citizen receiving payments. Trump could responsibly lead as Reagan did in 1982 to implement reforms that would stabilize the system. Instead, he chose to join the ostrich caucus with Biden and adopt a position of “No changes; Not now; Not ever.” Shame on both of them.

Trump’s pettiness and impetuousness has combined to literally put former high ranking American officials in physical danger. He removed the security details of former National Security Advisor John Bolton and former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, even though the world, and specifically Iran, knows that they were involved in planning the Trump-ordered assassination of high-ranking Iranian military officials.

Think about that. The president publicly orders that former high-ranking American officials who helped carry out his orders should be placed in physical danger because … why? Is that an acceptable action to you as an American citizen?

Trump has also recently taken to labeling certain Democrats as socialists. Undoubtedly, some of them are. But for the leader of a party that has taken partial ownership in 31 private corporations it is indeed rich to castigate others as socialistic. You may recall a principle of socialism: government ownership of the means of production. Trump has apparently adopted it as his standard mode of operation.

True conservatives are realizing that Trump is using the Republican Party for his own convenience. Trump’s presidency seems rooted in a policy du jour mindset which responds first and foremost to pleasuring his insatiable ego.

America will survive this “all about me” presidency. If my beloved Republican Party wants to survive it, it must return to its conservative roots of small government, personal freedoms, peace through strength, moral leadership of freedom-loving people and especially respect for our constitutional principles.

Kevin Igoe is the former deputy chief of staff of the Republican National Committee and former executive director of the Maryland Republican Party. He served as chief of staff of the Maryland Department of Budget and Management and was a Reagan White House appointee.

articles.title: Warren warns of ‘enormous risk’ if Musk is ‘dictating our foreign policy’
articles.summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) says there needs to be an investigation of who ordered the limit on Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite-based internet network and warned there is an “enormous risk” if Elon Musk is “dictating our foreign policy” by deciding what tools Ukraine has on the battlefield. “We’d like to know exactly who…
articles.body:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) says there needs to be an investigation of who ordered the limit on Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite-based internet network and warned there is an “enormous risk” if Elon Musk is “dictating our foreign policy” by deciding what tools Ukraine has on the battlefield.

“We’d like to know exactly who is responsible for what happened,” Warren told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins when asked about Ukraine’s loss of access to the satellite network it needs to operate drones and other military craft.

“If it is one man, Elon Musk, who is dictating our foreign policy, then he puts the United States at enormous risk,” Warren, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, warned.

“He’s the one who decides whether or not Ukraine is out there fighting on the front lines to protect its democracy lives or dies? No, we should not have one man in that position,” she argued.

Warren made her comments after the Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX, which created Starlink and its military-oriented sister company Starshield, ordered a restriction on Ukraine’s data speeds.

The restriction on Ukraine’s access to Starshield hampered its ability to fly drones and other military vehicles to counter Russian drone attacks.

The Journal reported that Musk and Trump discussed the decision to cap Ukraine’s access to Starlink shortly after the internet slowdown became public last week.

“If Donald Trump is the one who made this decision, then I will just say that’s one more reason we need a democratic majority in the House and the Senate so that we can actually put some constraints on Donald Trump, so that we can investigate and get to the bottom of this,” Warren said.

Other Democrats have criticized Musk in the wake of reports that he intervened to limit Ukraine’s ability to operate drones at a time when Russia has escalated strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and civilian targets.

“Elon Musk shouldn’t have the power to influence the outcome of a war with the flip of a switch. Yet he and Trump seem determined to put their finger on the scale for Putin,” Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.), a senior member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, posted on X.

Musk, in s social media post last week, said that Starshield is operated by the Department of Defense and that Trump ultimately has the authority to decide whether to limit data speeds for Ukraine or other users.

His comment appeared to point the finger at the Pentagon for Ukraine’s loss of Starshield access.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk posted on X, the social media platform, which he owns.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday suggested Musk’s company was responsible, suggesting Ukraine had violated its “terms of service.”

“We haven’t pulled anything back,” Hegseth told reporters of Ukraine’s access to Musk’s satellites. “There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions.”

A bipartisan group of senators including four Republicans — Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) — have asked the Defense Department’s inspector general to investigate if any senior Pentagon officials ordered or had advance knowledge of restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield.

articles.title: GTA 6 launch could drain $1 billion from US economy — this is how
articles.summary: Economics professor Jose Garcia Montalvo calculated the figure using an estimated 1.5 million workers calling out sick on release day.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — As the video game industry prepares for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI next month, the highly anticipated launch could have a significant economic impact, with many Americans saying they plan to call out sick to play it.

The International Business Times reported that economics professor José García Montalvo estimates a mass sick day tied to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI could cost the U.S. economy nearly $1 billion.

Montalvo calculated the figure using an estimated 1 1/2 million workers calling out sick and an average annual output of about $70,000 per worker, according to the report.

The publication added that when Grand Theft Auto V was released in 2013, reports found that as many as 6% of workers aged 18 to 35 in cities such as Los Angeles and New York took the day off to play the game.

Fans of the long-running crime-action series have eagerly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI since Rockstar Games unveiled it in February 2022.

The game, currently available for preorder, costs $79.99 and will follow the adventures of a criminal couple as they navigate the fictional state of Leonida, Rockstar said .

Originally slated for release in 2025 , Grand Theft Auto VI has been delayed multiple times and serves as the long-awaited sequel to 2013’s Grand Theft Auto V.

NewsNation’s Zach Kaplan contributed to this report.

articles.title: 2026 midterms: 7 key governor races to watch and where they stand
articles.summary: DDHQ’s forecast, last updated Oct. 17, has Democrats favored in 20 of the 36 races, with four rated as toss-ups.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With early voting underway in several states, 36 governorships are on the ballot Nov. 3.

Decision Desk HQ ‘s forecast (as of Oct. 18) has Democrats favored in 21 of the 36 races, with four rated as toss-ups.

These are the races to watch this November.

Billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson spent nearly $100 million of his own money to win the Republican nomination, beating Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, 53% to 47%.

The latest DDHQ forecast shows Jackson narrowly behind Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, at 55% to 45%.

If elected, Lance Bottoms would be Georgia’s first female and first Black governor , and possibly the first Black woman elected to governor anywhere in the U.S. A win would make her the first Democrat elected governor since Roy Barnes in 1998.

Democrat Amy Acton is favored with a 60%-win probability over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, according to DDHQ’s forecast .

Trump rallied for Ramaswamy in Youngstown Oct. 12. Former President Barack Obama is scheduled to campaign with Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown in Cleveland Oct. 24.

If she wins, Acton would be the first Democratic gubernatorial victory in Ohio since Ted Strickland in 2006.

Nevada is DDHQ’s closest governor’s race in the country. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo faces Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford, with Lombardo holding a 51%-win probability, according to DDHQ .

Ford has hammered the incumbent on the cost of living and his ties to Trump. Data centers have become a dominant issue, as 80% of the state’s land is owned by the federal government.

State Auditor Rob Sand is the only Democrat holding statewide office in Iowa, which hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since Chet Culver in 2006. He faces Republican Zach Lahn this November.

DDHQ’s forecast has Sand with a 73%-win probability.

Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson leads Republican Rep. John James with a 76%-win probability to succeed term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer , according to DDHQ’s forecast .

Her running mate, state Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, would make it Michigan’s first all-female ticket, and Republicans haven’t won the governorship since 2014.

Gov. Kathy Hochul is a clear favorite over Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, with a 91% win probability , according to DDHQ. The two met Oct. 13 in their only scheduled debate , where they sparred over immigration, Trump and living costs.

Democrat Xavier Becerra faces Republican Steve Hilton to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom. Becerra would be California’s first Latino governor since the late 1800s. No Republican has been elected governor in California since Arnold Schwarzenegger.

Becerra holds a 96% win probability over Hilton, according to DDHQ.

articles.title: Not just gas and groceries: Childcare costs weigh on voters before midterm elections
articles.summary: About three-quarters of U.S. adults saw the expense of childcare as a “major problem” in the U.S.
articles.body:
Like so many Americans, Jenny Escolastico has watched wearily as the cost of living has risen, straining her household budget. But as a mother of two children under 5, she faces added pressure that could shape how she votes in November : childcare costs.

Escolastico’s household outside Allentown, Pennsylvania, is relying solely on her husband’s income. She’s staying home with her children, at least in part because she simply can’t afford to work .

“What I would be spending on childcare would be more than what I would be making if I were working full time,” said Escolastico, an Air Force veteran who later worked in human resources. “Childcare is another rent, another car note.” Even though her son now attends state-funded prekindergarten , returning to work would still mean finding him after-school care, plus full-time childcare for her daughter.

Those costs are top of mind as Escolastico, who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, weighs whether to vote Democratic next month.

She lives in Pennsylvania’s hotly contested 7th Congressional District, one of a handful that will determine which party controls Congress next year. The midterm elections have been dominated by anxiety over rising prices for gas, groceries and housing, a liability for Trump and his Republican Party. For millions of parents of young children, childcare is one of the largest strains on the family budget.

Both parties are talking about childcare

Childcare costs rose faster than inflation from 2020 to 2024, with the U.S. average for full-time childcare topping $13,000 in 2025, according to Child Care Aware of America. About three-quarters of U.S. adults saw the expense of childcare as a “major problem” in the U.S., and 64% supported the federal government providing free- or low-cost childcare for children too young for public school, according to an AP-NORC poll from June 2025.

In the 7th District north of Philadelphia, both candidates are making childcare part of their pitch to voters. Like Escolastico, about 16% of the district’s voters were undecided as of September, according to a poll from Franklin and Marshall College .

Democratic nominee Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter, has campaigned on establishing universal prekindergarten, expanding full-day kindergarten, increasing funding for Head Start and making more working families eligible for federal childcare assistance. He’s cited his own experience pitching in on childcare for his two granddaughters.

“The cost of caring for the people you love keeps climbing, and nobody in Washington seems to notice,” Brooks said in a news release.

The incumbent, freshman Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, himself a father of two kids under age 3, has embraced more modest approaches that rely on tax breaks to lower costs.

He cosponsored a bill to expand the federal tax credit for childcare expenses. The proposal, ultimately folded into Trump’s sweeping bill of tax breaks and cuts to social programs, also increased tax incentives for private employers who subsidize or provide childcare for their workers.

“I will continue to work together with both sides to ensure that working families get the resources, representation, and support that they deserve,” Mackenzie said in a statement.

Trump himself had campaigned on cutting childcare costs by using tariff revenue, a plan that has yet to materialize. More recently, he expressed skepticism of federal money for childcare.

“We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare,” Trump told an Easter luncheon.

Childcare has become an increasingly urgent priority

The urgency over early childhood policy was accelerated by the pandemic. Daycare closures and weekslong quarantines laid bare the necessity and financial precarity of the childcare industry. To keep providers open, the federal government spent more than $50 billion on the industry, funding staff training, higher wages, protective gear and childcare assistance for more families.

In 2021, President Joe Biden, a Democrat, proposed offering subsidies to most American families so they would never pay more than 7% of their household income on childcare. It was narrowly defeated in Congress.

Three years later, the last of the pandemic aid expired. Waitlists for childcare assistance exploded, forcing low-income households to sideline a parent from the workforce or forgo necessities to foot a childcare bill.

Since then, more candidates have campaigned on childcare solutions. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, pledged to make childcare free for all residents. The Democratic governors of New Jersey and Virginia elected last year both campaigned on plans to increase childcare funding. The Democratic nominee for mayor in Washington, D.C., won the primary in June after proposing to cap childcare expenses at 7% of a household’s income.

With childcare prices rising, Lerin Hagenbuch of Allentown says she wonders why the country hasn’t moved toward universal childcare. She recalled when she and her husband, a quality assurance manager, anxiously searched for childcare so she could return to her job as a special education teacher, only to find that some of their options would require her to take a second job.

Her son is now in kindergarten, but childcare costs remain one of her top issues. She’s a registered Republican, but hasn’t decided how to vote next month.

“There are staff shortages everywhere,” Hagenbuch said. “If these moms or dads who are staying at home were able to even work part time, what a shift that would be.”

$60 million in election spending boosts childcare issues

The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, which advocates for greater government support for paid leave, child care and elder care, hopes voters like Hagenbuch will side with Democrats, who have historically favored bigger-ticket childcare investments.

The political action committee said it has spent $60 million this year backing Democrats in statehouse, congressional and governor’s races, targeting voters in a dozen states with canvassing, ads and mailers. The campaign pursues voters from both parties who feel the cost of caring for a child or an aging parent is growing untenable.

“This is something that every family is touched by,” said Phoebe Kilgour, the campaign’s deputy executive director. “And so when you talk to people about what candidates are gonna do to … lower the cost of care, it can be super persuasive.”

A longtime preschool teacher, Becky Fisher of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, earns less than $20 an hour. Much of her paycheck goes to pay for before- and after-school care for her two sons at the childcare center where she works.

Fisher was raised in a conservative Christian household and registered as a Republican when she graduated from high school, voting for President George W. Bush’s reelection. She switched parties and in 2024 voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats’ unsuccessful nominee for president.

This year, she’s still deciding how to vote, but says she wants to back a congressional candidate who will do more than pay lip service to supporting families and teachers. Childcare and early education are among the lowest-paid professions in the nation. And many of the field’s workers are parents like her.

“Every parent is exhausted,” Fisher said.
